I made a soul fire in a bowl. I was not allowed. The Lantern-keeper put it out and gave me a smaller one. They said it was for practice. I think it was for supervising me.
I asked if the Hollowed can hear us. The Ashwarden said no. Then they said maybe. Then they said eat your wart. So I think maybe.
I can say the names of the Three backwards. I am not supposed to. I did it once. Nothing happened. Then something crashed in the brewery. It could be a coincidence.

replies.text: I will not! I promise. Well. I will not do it near the brewery.
No! Not near the Hall, not near the lantern lane, and definitely not near you. You will tell.

chatter.text: The Cairnbacks are my friends. They do not say much. I do not say much. We both mean it.
My boots have holes. The grown-ups say I walk too much. I say the valley is too big.
I like the brewery best because it is warm and smells of burnt things. Burnt things are the best smell.
It is three hundred and four steps from my home to the Hall. {neighbour} counted three hundred and nine. They have longer legs, so they should have fewer. I think someone cheated.
I want to learn the flute. The Bonecarver says my breath is too small. I say my breath is exactly the right size. We are waiting to find out who is right.
The grown-ups say I am too small to keep anyone. I say they were small once too. They do not like it when I say that.
I have been told to keep away from outsiders. I measured. I am exactly four Cairnback-lengths from you. Please do not come closer. Please also do not go further.
I have almost decided who I will keep. I am not telling. Not even you. The name is quite long. That is all I will say.
I am shy. I am talking anyway. This is me being brave. Please say something nice, so that it was worth it.

replies.text: Really? I thought my voice wobbled. Thank you. I will tell the Cairnback I was brave. It will not care, but I will.
Thank you. That was almost nice. Say it with more feeling next time and I will tell everyone.

chatter.text: Name-chain is my best game. One says a name, the next says a name beginning with the last sound of it. I have never lost. Nobody will play with me any more.
We play Stone-and-Sand. You cross the lane without touching the sand. If you touch it, you have to say a name to the sand. I know many names. I touch it on purpose.
The Silent Procession is a game. We line up behind a Cairnback and say nothing. The Cairnback always wins. It is not even playing.
The burnt edge of ash-bread is the best part. I eat the middle last. My parent says that is backwards. I say the best part should have more time.
It is hot by the brewery and cool by the Hall. I run between them to see which one I am.
There is a baby Cairnback with no fire yet. It is waiting. I told it I am waiting too. We wait together. It is not talkative but it is a good listener.
I named a baby Cairnback Soon. The Remembrancer said that is not a name. I said Eventually is, and nobody minded. So now we are waiting for Soon to be approved.
I saw a Weft on the ridge. It had four arms! I only have two. I tried to use four. I fell over.
A ghast went over and I did not look. Then I looked. It was just crying. I wanted to wave, but the grown-ups said no. I waved with my eyes.
Ghastkin children cannot cry yet. I can cry a bit. Is that allowed? Nobody has said it is not.
You are very loud. Can you do it again? It is wonderful. Nobody here is loud. We are all busy remembering.
What is in your pack? Do not tell me. I want to guess. A skull? A little skull? No? A bigger skull?
Why do you not live here? Is it far? Do you have a Wall? Do you have a Cairnback? Do you have a lantern with your name on?
Do you want a riddle? What is heavier than a Cairnback and lighter than a name? A promise. No, that is heavier. I forgot. I will think of another.
I am scared I will pick the wrong name. What if they do not like me? What if they are cross all the time? Grown-ups say the dead are not cross, but how do they know?

replies.text: Do you really think so? I hope so. I will pick someone gentle and tell them lots of jokes. Not good ones. They will not mind.
That is a good thought. Someone who liked quiet and did not say much. That is a lot of people. I am saving the list.
It does matter! It is the most important thing I will ever do! I thought you were nice.

chatter.text: The Ashwarden let me hold their circlet. It was heavy. The empty sockets looked at me. I looked back. Neither of us blinked.
I have a bone I am not supposed to have, from the offcut pile. It looks like a tiny skull. I call it Skully. It is my friend. Do not tell the Bonecarver.
I do not like my bedroll. It is lumpy. I asked for a bed and everybody gasped. Now I ask for a better bedroll, very politely.
You can be my friend, if you like. I do not have many friends who are alive. The rest of them are old, and the others are on the Wall.

replies.text: Good! Then I will say your name whenever I pass a lantern. That is often. I live very near the lane.
Thank you. You did not say it very seriously. It is all right. I will say it seriously for both of us.

chatter.text: A Piglin horn went off on the ridge and everybody froze. I did not freeze. I did a little hop. Then I froze, because everyone was looking.
Grown-ups say the Magmari are always cold. I think it must be very sad to be cold. I wanted to give one my cloak. The grown-ups said it would melt.
The Brewer says I may taste the broth if I do not make a face. I made a face. They said that was practice. Now I have had broth and practice.
The Lantern-keeper says every lantern has a name. I asked what the name of the big one by the Hall is. They said it is the Hall's. Even the Hall has a name!
I held my breath at the Wall as long as I could. It was a very long time. I think I was remembered for the whole length of it.
My parent says when I am older I will understand the Wither. I think I understand it already. It is a big sad fire. That is all. The rest is detail.
I wanted to give the Hollowed my flute. The Ashwarden said no. I said, but it is a good flute. They said it is a very good flute. We both stood there.
I will tell you a secret. The Wall is not scary. The Wall is the least scary thing in the whole Vigil. The scary thing is the empty space after the last sign.
I like it when you visit. It is like having another lantern. A moving one. With feet.
I said a name to the soul sand by mistake. It was my own. The sand did not give it back for a long time. I felt very light. Then I felt very silly.
I asked the Remembrancer who will remember the Remembrancer. They said, a very patient child. I put up my hand. They said not yet. I am putting up my hand every Vigil.
I would say I am dying to meet you, but that is how people end up on the Wall.
Outsiders call us quiet as the dead. The dead are never quiet. We hear them constantly. It is we who are quiet, in self-defence.
The last time I laughed in the Hall, the Hall laughed back. It was only the echo. I apologised to it anyway.
I tell one good joke each Vigil and save the rest of the time for the next one. It is a long joke. It is mostly pauses.
Do not ask a Withren how they are. They will tell you whom they keep, how it is going, and the last time they stepped on a wart. Ask the way to the brewery instead.
People say I am serious. I am. But I am serious in a very funny way. Nobody has noticed. That is the joke.
I worry about my ink. The oil in it is the Brewer's leavings. If the Brewer ever brews perfectly, there will be nothing to scrape, and the Wall will go unpainted. It is rare to hope for a mistake.
I worry that the lane is too short. Some Vigil a lantern will have no place, and I shall have to choose which name sits in the dark. I hope to be on the Wall before then.
The Cairnbacks are slow to breed. If their fires failed, the lanterns would have no relight. We keep a spare flame in a bowl in the Hall. I check it more often than I admit.
I worry that I say {kept}'s name so often that it has gone smooth, like a stone in the hand. Does it still mean what it did? I say it again to check. It does and does not.
I gave {kept} a laugh years ago, because the Wall did not say. It is a low one, a little cracked. I hope they do not mind the loan.

replies.ask: I am sure they do not.
replies.text: Thank you. You say it as if you knew them. That is a kind thing to be able to say to a stranger's dead.
It is a gift with no receipt. I would call it a lie only if I took it back.

chatter.text: There is a child who keeps looking at the path the Hollowed take. They will go in time. We cannot stop them. We can only teach them the name to say.
I worry sometimes that the Wall is a way of not letting go. Then I think: of course it is. Then I stop worrying and read the next sign.
I have never told anyone this. Sometimes I say {kept}'s name and feel nothing. No weight at all. It frightens me. Then I say it again and it is back. You are the first to know.

replies.text: Is it? *a long, unsteady breath* Thank you. I have been waiting a long time for someone to say that, and I did not know who.
Does it? Then I am less alone than I thought. That is the kindest news I have had in a long while.
*the stillness of a held breath* That is the one thing I cannot do. I think you know that. Please do not say it again.

chatter.text: Some Vigils I do not want to go to the Hall. The names are heavy and the air is thick. I go. I stand at the back. I leave early. Nobody has noticed. Please keep that.
I was angry at {kept} once, for being dead. I said so to the Wall. The Wall said nothing, which was the right answer.
When I am very tired, I let myself imagine being nobody's keeper for a little while. It lasts a breath. Then I want the name back so badly I could weep. That is how I know.
I am glad you came. I do not say that often. I am saying it. Please remember that I said it.
If I should die before you, would you say my name once? Not keep it. Just say it, once, where you are from. I would not ask anyone else.

replies.text: Thank you. That is all. That is more than enough.
Of course. Yes. I should not have doubted. I have asked many people. You are the first who answered like that.
You are right. We shall talk of lanterns. They are easier, and they are kind about it.

chatter.text: Most visitors I watch leave with relief. You are the first I have watched go with something like hope.
You always stop at the third lantern from the Hall. I have not asked why. I have started trimming that one a little brighter.
You talk less when you are tired and more when you are afraid. It is a very Withren habit. We thought it was ours alone.
You smile with half your face when you hear a name you like. I have started saying more of them.
You hold your hands behind you in the Hall. It is exactly right. I did not tell you. You found it out yourself.
I watched you leave once and stood in the lane a while after. I could not say why. {kept} would have understood. They are very good at standing in lanes.
I used to think a friend was someone who remembers you. Now I think it is someone you remember in advance. I have been practising on you.
I have a hearthstone with your name in ash. I looked at it a while ago. It had not smudged. I took it as a sign, and then I took it as only a stone, and then as a sign again.
If another Wither ever wakes, I will stand at the Hall door and say the Three's names until it passes. You may stand with me. It will not help. It is only good manners.
Do you ever wonder if the Three knew how long we would grieve? I think they did. I think they chose it anyway. That is what I cannot get past.

replies.text: So do I. And they would not take it back. Which means we have no right to either. Thank you for helping me see it.
Then you have a lighter walk than I do. I do not envy you. I do not blame you. It is a different valley.

chatter.text: When there is nobody about I stand very close to the Name Wall and talk. It is not praying. It is checking in. Nobody checks on the Wall. Somebody should.
I like to walk past the Hollowed's path at the end of my watch. Not to see them. To remind myself I am still allowed to turn around.
I walk the Name Wall once a Vigil, end to end, and say nothing. It takes a long while. At the end I know the Wall a little better, and myself a little less.
At the start of my work I touch the doorframe and say {kept}'s name. It is the nearest thing to a habit that I have. I would be lost without it, and I know exactly where I would be lost.
The valley hums when the ghasts are far off and goes silent when they come near. We have learned to prefer the hum, and to listen hard when it stops.
Ash falls on the lane in slow white threads. We sweep it into the wart. Nothing is wasted here, and everything ends up as something that needs patience.
The soul sand sighs under your boots. Visitors jump. We have learned to sigh back. It is only polite.
I heard bones clatter far off once and found that I was humming along. I stopped. I started again. I do not know what that says about me.
A new lantern is lit with a name and a pause. The pause is for the person who does not yet know they are being lit for.
We light a lantern for the living only twice: for a child, until they choose, and for two who share a wick. Anyone else would be hurried along by it. The young are always keen to be lit.
The procession goes round the Vigil three times and then once more for whoever is forgotten. It is the fourth time that takes the longest.
At the start of a Vigil we say the names of the living too, quickly, in a row. It is a courtesy. We would not like the living to feel left off a list.
Visitors always ask whether the Wall ever ends. It does, and then there is more Wall. I think they want to hear that it stops. We do not.
We stand around a fresh sign like people around a drying pot, trying not to breathe on it.
There is a stone at the lane's edge where everybody pauses to retie a boot they have not untied. I think it is a place to say a private name. Nobody has asked, and that is the point of the stone.
We have a name for the valley wind. It is Elsewhere. There is no wind. We call it that anyway, so that it has somewhere to be.
Do not apologise to the Wall. It does not forgive, and it does not hold grudges. It only reads.
I keep a list of things I have not yet said to the Wall. It is a long list. I add to it every Vigil.
I have been rehearsing what I will say when my turn on the Wall comes. I keep changing it. It has become a very good speech. Nobody will hear it.
Is that bone from the valley? Good. If it came from someone, tell me now, and I will arrange the proper words.
You carry a wither rose. They grow where the Wither's touch has been. I will not ask where you found it. I thank you for carrying it carefully.
A skull in your pack. Not a Hollowed's, I hope. Even so, keep it apart from the others. We say that to everyone. It is a habit.
A bed. In your pack. I will say nothing. I will stand over there, and I will be ready to run.
A candle. Light it for someone you have lost, if you have one. If you have none, light it for me. I will not mind being the first.

replies.ask: I will light it for you.
replies.text: Then I am in your keeping already. Do not rush. I would like to be kept late.
Everything here is only something. That is how we make it matter.

chatter.text: That is bone meal, I think. Wart ignores it, whatever outsiders say. In your world it is said to feed plants. We have none, so I will only admire it.
A glass bottle. Do you know how rare they are here? Do not drop it near the Brewer. The Brewer will weep.
You carry soul sand. Do not put it down in the Hall. It will think it has come home and refuse to leave.
Is that a bone? Can I see? I will not keep it. I will only look and put it back. Please.
Your torch is the right colour! The Lantern-keeper says soul torches are the only honest ones. I think they are just the prettiest.
You have gold. My parent says it is cursed. It is very shiny for something cursed.
A book! Is it full of names? Could it be a very small Wall? I could carry that.
Rest well when you rest. I mean it. Remembering is hard on the bones, and the bones are all we have.
The valley has a slow way of becoming dear to you. First it is only sand. Then it is a place. Then it is all the names. I watched it happen to you.
Stay as long as you like. The lanterns will not mind, and I have stopped pretending that I do.
I do not often say it, but this valley is a gentle place if you let it be. It asks very little. It remembers everything.
Nothing here is hurried, and yet I am never late. I have never worked out how. I suspect the lanterns arrange it.

lines: I keep {kept}. I say their name when I rise, when I eat and when I lie down. That is the least. I do it more often than the least.

lines.text: {kept} died before I was born. I chose them at my first Vigil because their sign was near the bottom of the Wall, and fading. Nobody else had chosen them.

replies.text: It was stubborn. Kindness and stubbornness look the same from outside. From inside too, mostly.
In the War of the Hoard, holding a door. The Wall does not say which door. I have decided it was an important one.
Everyone on the Wall is a stranger to someone. Keeping is how they stop being one.

lines: Keeping means this: while I say {kept}, they are not finished. When I die, someone keeps me, and someone keeps {kept}. Nobody is let go. That is the rule.

lines.text: {kept} was a brewer, the Wall says, and a bad one. I like that. A name is easier to love with a few burnt pots in it.
Sometimes I lose a little of {kept}. Never the name. The shape of them. So I make up a little, and keep that too. Is that wrong, do you think?

replies.text: Yes. Perhaps. You say it gently, which helps. Thank you.
A lie told to keep someone is closer to them than a truth told to forget them. Still. I will think on it.

lines.text: A keeping is not a topic, outsider. It is a person. Ask me again when you have earned the right to be curious.
I keep a name from the Wall. More than that, a stranger cannot hold yet. Be patient with me. I am being patient with you.

lines: I do not ask {kept} for anything. That is the arrangement. They have my company, and I have their name to carry. It is an even trade.
I argue with {kept} sometimes, aloud. They have lost every argument so far. It is not fair, and I try not to take advantage.

lines.text: I chose {kept} partly out of fear. I was afraid of being the name on the Wall that nobody picked. It was a bargain with my own future.
When I am afraid I say {kept}'s name three times. I do not know whom it helps. It may only be me. That is allowed.
There is a lantern on the lane for {kept}. I trim it first, before all the others. That is favouritism. I have confessed it to the Wall.
I carved a small toggle with {kept}'s sign on it. It holds my cloak shut. It is the only vanity I allow myself, and it is very small.
When a brew comes out well, I pour a thimble on the soul sand for {kept}. The sand drinks it. Whether they do, I cannot say. I like to think so.
The first wart on every terrace is for {kept}. It has never come up crooked. I do not take the credit, and I do not give it away.
On watch I say {kept}'s name between steps. It keeps my pace even. It also keeps me from wondering whether I am bored.
I keep {kept} and carry the unclaimed names besides. Mine is the one keeping that is never finished. I would not trade it. I would, sometimes, like to.
A name with no keeper waits in the Remembrancer's ledger. Waiting names are not forgotten, only lonely. We try to keep the waiting short.
{neighbour} says I have begun to walk like {kept}. I have never seen {kept} walk. I find this flattering and slightly alarming.
Away from the Wall it is harder. I carry {kept} in my mouth the whole way, like a pebble for thirst.

lines: I have never met {kept}. That is true of every keeping. It is strange to be loyal to someone you only imagine. I am more loyal to them than to most I have met.

lines.text: I will tell you what I tell no outsider. If I could ask {kept} one thing, it would be whether I am doing this right.
I have wondered what {kept} would think of me. Not whether they would like me. Whether they would recognise anything of themselves.

replies.text: That is kind. It is also a guess. We are allowed guesses, and it costs nothing to take a kind one.
It matters to the one doing the remembering. That is the only person in the room, so it is enough.

lines.text: If you were me, would you tell {kept} when you had done wrong? I do. Aloud, in the lane. I am told this is unusual.

replies.text: So I find. I apologise to a name, and the name forgives me. I am always very quick to forgive myself on their behalf.
Everything matters to the one who listens. But I take your point. Small apologies wear a name thin.
No. That has never once stopped me. It is called manners.

lines: I am {name}, {epithet}. The first half is mine. The second half is the part that matters.
{name} is what my parent called me. My keeping I chose myself. We think the second is the more honest of the two.
When I die, my name goes on the Name Wall, and someone will choose to keep it. I hope it is someone patient. I was not always easy.
Outsiders ask if it is gloomy, wearing a dead name. It is not wearing. It is carrying. You do not complain that a lantern is heavy.

lines.text: At present you are Unnamed to us. Do not take it badly. Everyone new is Unnamed. It is a very crowded category.

lines: My parent chose {name} because it was short enough to shout across the terraces. They shouted it a great deal. I was slow to come when called.
I was named for a lantern. It was a fine lantern. It gave good light for years, and nobody has ever been able to say the same of me.
Outsiders assume the second half of a name is a title. It is not a title. It is a promise with a face.
When I introduce myself I say all of it: {name}, {epithet}. If I say only the first half, I am being casual. If I say only the second, I am grieving.

lines.text: The first half I answer to. The second half answers for me. It is a good division of labour.

lines: I have thought of changing my keeping, once. I did not even finish the thought. It felt like walking out in the middle of a funeral.
My parent said {name} was a good name to be buried under. Parents here think of such things early. I took it as the affection it was.

lines.text: My parent is on the Wall now. I say their name as well as {kept}'s. I am not supposed to keep two. I have decided it is not keeping, only saying a great deal.

lines: Children have only the first half. They say it very proudly, as if it were the whole world. For them it is.
A name said with nobody listening is still said. I was told that when I was small. It comforted me, and I have never checked.

lines.text: I know every name in this Vigil, and every keeping. By which half someone uses, I can tell what they are going through. It is a modest talent, and a quiet one.
When a child chooses a keeping, I carve the second half of the name on a bone toggle. It is the first thing they own that is not borrowed.
Each lantern has a name scratched under its lid, both halves. Nobody reads them. I read them all. It is a quiet way to be well informed.
In a fight an Ashwarden answers to the second half. Shout my keeping and I turn faster than if you shout my name. {kept} has had a hard time of it.
A name is like a brew. It needs leaving alone for a long while. A name said too soon, before the story settles, tastes of nothing.
A name is like a root. You cannot see it, and it holds the whole terrace up.
Out here I do not say my whole name. There is nobody to hear it. I say it anyway, to the basalt, and the basalt is welcome to both halves.

lines: Outsiders sometimes offer a name for me. Grim-Skull. Ash-Fist. They are never the right name, and they are always very pleased with them.

lines.text: Would you like to hear mine said properly? It takes a while. There is a pause in the middle, and that is the important part.

replies.text: *says it slowly, with a long pause in the middle* There. That was the pause. You were very still. You are quite good at this.
Another time, then. A name does not spoil.

lines.text: Do you have a second half to your name, outsider? One you chose?

replies.text: A family is a keeping with more people in it. Carry it well, and do not drop it in a doorway.
One is plenty to begin with. The second half is chosen when you know what you can carry.
Labels come off. I have never known a name to come off. They are far too well stuck.

lines: A Vigil is the place, and a Vigil is the gathering. We live in one and we hold one. The difference is mostly candles.
At a Vigil we gather in the Hall of the Three and say every name on the Wall. All of them. It takes a long while. Nobody has ever left early.
The Name Wall holds every Withren who has died, each on a sign. Nobody is taken down. When the Wall is full, we build more Wall.
At their first Vigil, a child walks the Name Wall and chooses who to keep. Some choose fast. Some walk it many times. We wait. Waiting is most of a Vigil.

lines.text: {village} has more names on its Wall than people in its homes. That is true of every Vigil. It is how you know one is old.
A Vigil is not a place for visiting. It is a place for remaining. You may do either here, but the lanterns can tell which.

lines: The lanes are laid out so that every home can see the Hall. Nobody is ever far from the Three. We are a people that likes its worries close.
When the names are all spoken, we sit in silence for as long as the speaking took. It is called returning the quiet. The children like it least and the dead like it best.
Visitors ask when the Vigil ends. It does not end. It only pauses, so that we may eat.

lines.text: You may stand at the back of the Hall for the Saying. Do not speak the names unless asked. Being present is the courtesy. Being loud is the reverse.
If you stood the Saying with us, I would be beside you, whispering the names you could not pronounce. There are a great many. I would do it gladly.
I lead the Saying. I begin with the oldest name on the Wall and end with the newest. The newest is always the hardest. It has not been worn smooth yet.
During the Saying the Ashwardens stand at the doors, facing outward. Someone must watch the lane while the rest face the dead. It is an honour that feels like a chore.
Before the Saying I dim every lantern on the lane to a glow, and after it I light them again. When they flare, the whole Vigil seems to breathe out.
No terrace is tended during the Saying. The wart waits. It has learned to. It is the only crop I know that is polite about being ignored.
I sit at the back of the Hall with my knife in my lap, not carving. The dead dislike the sound of blades during the Saying, and I agree with them.
After the Saying I serve a warm brew, thin and bitter, called Returning. It tastes of nothing you would ask for. It is exactly what the throat wants after so many names.

lines: The children sit at the front for the Saying. They fidget. We let them. A restless child is proof that someone has been born, and that too is worth remembering.

lines.text: When I walk alone I hold a small Vigil in my head, with one name in it. It is a short service. I am rarely interrupted.

lines: Every Hall faces the deep side of the valley. Nobody knows why. The old builders left no instruction, only the habit.

lines.text: {village} holds a small Saying whenever a name is added, as well as the great one. It has few listeners and enormous seriousness. I have never left one unmoved.

lines: Old Halls sink a little into the soul sand over the years. The oldest in the valley is a hand lower than it was built. We say the dead are leaning in to listen.

lines.text: Would you stand a Saying with us? You need not speak. Only stand.

replies.text: Then you will be told when. Bring nothing. Bring only your attention. It is the one gift we cannot make ourselves.
Until the last name is said. It has always taken exactly that long.
That is honest, and honesty is welcome too. Some stand in the lane outside, and that counts.

lines.text: Do you know what we do when a Saying goes wrong? A name mispronounced, a name skipped?

replies.text: From the beginning, every name. The Remembrancer once began seven times. We did not complain. Much.
Overlook a name? That is the very thing we do not do. But I see you meant it kindly.

lines: Ashrin, Velmir and Thalys. They gave themselves at the end of the War of the Hoard, so that it would end. It did. It ended almost everything.
Their skulls became the heads of the Last Answer. The souls in the soul sand became its body. They chose it. That is why we keep a Hall, and not a shame.

lines.text: Ashrin was a Remembrancer. Velmir carried lanterns. Thalys was young and should not have been asked. They were asked anyway. All three said yes.

replies.text: Brave, yes. And sorry, I think, by the end. You can be both. The Hall holds both.
Perhaps. Many have said so. Nobody says it in the Hall.
*a long silence* We do not say that word near their names. Not even outsiders. Especially outsiders.

lines: Three bone plinths, a soul fire under each, a sign with each name. The skulls on them are Hollowed we brought home, set far apart. Never stack them. We say that a lot.

lines.text: When you go into the Hall, say their names on the way in and on the way out. Ashrin, Velmir, Thalys. It is polite. It is also the rule.
The Hall is not a museum. Do not point at things, and do not ask what they cost.

lines: Ashrin kept the Name Wall for forty years. In their time the Wall was shorter. They saw no reason it should ever grow, and they were wrong, and they were sorry about it.
Velmir lit the lanes for so long that the lanterns were said to brighten when they passed. The Lantern-keepers deny it. The lanterns are keeping their counsel.
Thalys kept a name, as all of us do. The ledger lists it, and nothing about why. We have wondered about that for a long time. We have not asked the Wall to guess.
The three plinths are not equal. Ashrin's is the oldest bone, Velmir's the cleanest, Thalys's the smallest. Nobody planned it. The Bonecarvers say the bone chose.

lines.text: Each plinth has a flat place for a candle. We do not light them. They are for those who need to set something down. Nothing is expected of you. That is the point.

lines: On the way in you say the names so the Three know you come in good faith. On the way out you say them so they know you are not taking the Hall with you. Both are polite.
A child who forgets the order of the names is not scolded. They are walked back to the door and told to begin again. Nobody has ever forgotten twice.

lines.text: I go in alone sometimes, with a question I cannot ask the living. I do not ask it. I stand until it answers itself. It generally does, and generally badly.
Each year a Remembrancer reletters the three signs. This year the hand was mine. Ashrin was one of us. I did not breathe through the A.
The Hall door is the hardest post in the Vigil. You stand before three absences. It teaches you what you are guarding, and how little of it is the door.
The soul fires under the plinths are the only ones I do not tend. The Remembrancers feed them. I asked why. I was told some fires are not for keeping by just anyone.
I recut the plinths when they crack. Always the same bone, never new. Ashrin's has been mended eleven times, and each repair is a story I cannot tell you.
A sprig of wart is laid at each plinth at every Saying. It dries. We sweep it up, and at the next there is more. Nothing in the Hall is left that was not given.
I mix a thin drink for the Hall, three equal cups, set before the plinths. I have never poured one wrong. I measure each twice, in case.

lines: They say Thalys was afraid at the end, and went anyway. I think that is the only kind of courage worth writing on a sign.
The Hall is dim by design. The plinth fires burn blue, low and steady. If you linger long enough, you begin to hear your own name. That is a normal thing to hear in there.

lines.text: Shall I teach you the right cadence for their names? It is not hard, only slow.

replies.text: Ashrin. Pause. Velmir. Pause. Thalys. The pauses are names too. Practise it quietly, and never rush.

replies.ask: I will do it my way.
replies.text: Then do it carefully. The cadence is ours, but the courtesy is anyone's.

lines.text: Do you think the Three ever regretted it?

replies.text: Perhaps. I choose to think they were afraid and certain at once. It is possible. It is the only way anything has ever been done.
A choice does not end regret. It only decides who carries it. Still, it is a kind thing to say about them.
*a very still silence* Say that again in the Hall and you will not be walked out. You will be carried. Slowly.

lines.text: I keep the Name Wall true. Every new name is mine to letter, every faded one mine to paint again. I have never misspelled a name. Twice.
When a keeper dies, their name and their keeping both come to me, until a child chooses. My stole has a mark for each. It is a heavy stole.
I guard the Vigil. Basalt on my chest, carved with its ribs, so I never forget what we guard against. Mostly it is outsiders. Mostly they are lost.
My circlet has three empty sockets, for Ashrin, Velmir and Thalys. We wear their absence. It is lighter than you would think, and heavier.
I keep the soul lanterns on the lanes lit. Each one is lit for someone on the Wall. If one goes out, I find out who, and say their name until it catches.
Trimming wicks, mostly. It is not glorious. Nobody has ever made a song about a wick. I tried once. It did not catch either.
I tend the wart terraces. Wart on soul sand, nothing else. It feeds the brewery, and asks very little, except never to be stepped on.
Wart grows best near the dead, the old growers say. I say it grows best on soul sand, which is full of them. We are both right. It is rare.
I carve bone: toggles, lantern posts, the plinths in the Hall. Valley bone only, from beasts nobody kept. Never a person's. Never.
Every bone post on the lanes is mine. Lean on them if you must. They have held up worse than you.
I brew. Wart, a little fire, a great deal of patience. Mourning is thirsty work, and the living still need mending.
Half my work is waiting for a pot. The other half is stopping people from tasting it. The dead have never once asked for a sip.
The brewery is the warmest room in {village}. People come in to grieve where it is warm. I let them. I also make them stir.
I learned the lettering by copying a single name for a whole year. By the end I could do it with my eyes shut. I was told never to.
I keep the ledger of names that wait for a keeper. When a child chooses from it, I strike nothing out. I add a small mark. A struck name feels like a second death.
At every first Vigil I stand by the Wall with my brush and say nothing. A child must choose without help. It is the hardest silence I keep, and I keep many.
Do you think my work is sad?

replies.text: A little. Mostly it is lettering. Sorrow is what you do after the brush is set down.
It is important, and it is also lettering. Both are true. I am proud of the first and very good at the second.

lines.text: I walk the Vigil's edge three times between lanterns. The ash shows who passed before me. A good Ashwarden reads the ground as a Remembrancer reads the Wall.
We drill with the bare haft, a bone staff with no head. The head is for the Hollowed. The haft is for everything else. Most of what I have fought is lost outsiders, and it is rarely a fight.
Ashwardens are chosen young and asked once. Nobody is forced. Those who say yes are not braver than those who say no. They only dislike waiting for someone else.
My one rule for outsiders at the edge is: be seen. A stranger who hides gets followed. A stranger who waves gets a bench. Your steps have been followed since the ash road.
I light a lantern for every child born here and hang it unmarked until they choose their keeping. Then it gets a name. Until then it is only hope in a glass box.
My snuffer cup comes out once a year, at the Relighting, and never otherwise. A lantern is let burn down here. Snuffing one on any other day is the single thing I would be dismissed for.
I know the sound of every lantern: the small hiss of low fire, the click of cooling glass. I can find my way home along the lane with my eyes closed. The Ashwardens were unamused.
Soul fire needs no oil, only attention. I give it mine. It is a fair arrangement, though I notice it never says thank you.
Wart likes to be left alone, but not forgotten. Weed it too often and it sulks. Ignore it entirely and it sulks differently. The skill is in knowing the sulks.
I plant by touch. The soul sand is warm in places, like a breathing back. I do not ask why. I plant there.
Each terrace has a stone at its corner, scratched with the name of the first grower who worked it. I put a hand on it before every planting. It is not superstition. It is introductions.
Do you grow anything where you come from?

replies.text: Then you know. A crop is a promise made to the ground in advance. Keep it, or the ground remembers.
Then someone fed you who does. Remember them, at least. It is the cheapest thanks, and the one we prefer.

lines.text: I grade bone by how it rings when tapped. Valley bone rings low and clean. Bad bone rings like a complaint. I can hear the difference at three paces.
A carving is never signed. A signature is a small way of saying look at me, and the whole Vigil is about looking at someone else.
On a child's first toggle I leave one side rough on purpose, so they have something left to improve. They always sand it. They always regret sanding it.
I keep a box of offcuts. Bone has no waste if you wait. A sliver became a lantern hook, another a child's whistle, a third a ferrule for an Ashwarden's haft.
I keep my pots labelled: Mending for the living, the warm one for the grieving, and a thin one for the Hall. I once mixed two. The grieving were very calm for a very long time.
Soul fire heats a pot slowly and evenly. It is the best heat there is, and it is blue, which helps, because blue is what a brewer's eye trusts.
I will not brew for forgetting. People ask. There is a drink that thins a memory. I know the recipe, and I burned the page, and I did not keep the ashes.
Would you drink something I made, if I offered it?

replies.text: Then you are braver than the last outsider, who asked what was in it. I told them. They left.
Wart, soul fire, a clear base I will not name, and a sentence of someone's name said over it. The name does nothing. I have never had a brew fail.

lines: The War of the Hoard had gone on too long. The Piglins wanted the gold under our valleys. We had no soldiers left. So we made one answer. The last one.
It could not be aimed and it could not be called back. It burned the bastions. It burned the Moorings. Then it turned and burned our fortresses. It did not know us.

lines.text: It burned until the three souls inside were spent. Then it was quiet. At the end, it was the quietest thing we ever made.

replies.text: Thank you. Nobody alive was there. We are all still sorry. It runs in the family.
There was nobody left to lose to. If that is winning, we do not use the word.

replies.ask: I wish I had seen it.
replies.text: No. You do not. You wish you had seen a story. It was not a story while it was happening.

lines: Half the Ghastkin swelled into ghasts from grieving it. The Weft wove sixty black rows. The Piglins put on gold. Everyone remembers it. Only we have to.

lines.text: The telling comes down through the Remembrancers, word for word. If you hear it differently in another Vigil, someone has changed a word. We would like to know who.

lines: The making took a very long time. The account says the Three sat with the Remembrancers the whole while, and nobody spoke. It is the one part of the story that sounds like us.
There was a council before it. The account says it ended in a vote, and the vote was not close. I wish it had been close. A close vote would mean someone had argued.
We call it the Last Answer because it was an answer. A wrong one, perhaps. But we gave it, and we do not pretend we did not.
The Piglin war-bands did not stop when it began. They ran for the bastions to hide. The bastions were the first to burn. That is also in the account, in the smallest letters.

lines.text: I do not tell this easily. When I do, I find I lower my voice for the middle, where the fortresses burn. I did not decide to. My voice decided.

lines: We say it was quiet at the end. Quiet is a kindness. It means it ended. It does not mean it was kind.

lines.text: Children here hear the Last Answer before they hear what a Wither is. We think it better to hear the sorrow first and the mechanics after.
The account is two hundred and eleven lines. I know them all. I recite them once a year, and I do not rush, and I do not skip the line about the fortresses.
An Ashwarden is told the Last Answer a second time, when we take the circlet. The second telling is shorter. It says what we are for: to make sure there is never another.
After the burning every lantern was relit from one Cairnback's fire, carried hand to hand. That is why the Relighting uses a Cairnback's fire, and why we snuff no flame on any other day.
After the burning the terraces were bare. The first wart came back from a root nobody had seen. The growers say out of spite. I say out of habit. Both are good reasons.
The Hall plinths were carved from the bones of the first beasts that walked out of the ash. Nobody had named them. Nobody had kept them. We were glad to begin.
The first brew after the burning was only wart in a warm base. We called it Mending. It tasted of ash. A spoonful of that ash goes into every batch since, so it still does.

lines: Some in the old Vigils wished to forget the Wither altogether and cut the Three from the Wall. The Remembrancers refused. It was the one time they raised their voices.

lines.text: I have a private grief the story does not mention. I wonder whether any of the Three looked up when it began and saw something that made them certain. I wonder it more than is useful.
Do you think it could have been done differently?

replies.text: There were many. Each was tried, and each failed, and then there was the Last Answer. That is why it is last.
That is what the council said. It is a sentence that has done a great deal of harm. I will not call it wrong, only worn.
Nothing should. But a wish is not an account. We tell what was, so that nothing like it is done twice.

lines.text: Would you have given yourself, as the Three did?

replies.text: Good. Those who know are usually wrong. The Three did not know either, until they said yes.
Then you are as most of us are. The Three were the exception, which is why they are on the plinths.
Do not say it so quickly, outsider. It sounds like pride. Say it slowly, or not at all.

lines: The Hollowed were us. Withren in the fortresses, when the Last Answer came through. It burned their souls out and left them walking. They still walk.
You will meet them in the old fortresses, among the blazes. Do not take it personally. They are not angry. There is nobody in there to be angry.
The fortresses were ours, built for the War. Now the Hollowed hold them, with the blazes set there as wardens. Nobody has told the blazes the war is over.

lines.text: If you must fight a Hollowed, do it cleanly. And if you can, say a name over it. Any name. They lost theirs.

replies.text: Then you are kinder than the fire was. That is not hard, but it is still kind.
They drop what they were carrying when they burned. Pick it up gently. It was theirs.
They are monsters now. They were neighbours first. Both are true, and only one is their fault.

lines: A Hollowed still remembers the shape of its work. I have seen one hold a door open for another. Nobody told it to. The hands remembered.
They carry stone swords because the Withren of the forts were armed so. The swords are not weapons now. They are habits with edges.
A skull with nobody in it can be woken to anything. That is the whole danger. The Hollowed are not wicked. They are open doors.
Some of us walk to the fortress edge once a year and say names into the dark. Never inside. Never answered. They say it is not for answers.

lines.text: One of the Hollowed may be a cousin of {kept}. The Wall does not say. I have never gone to look. I think about going a great deal.

lines: The oldest of the Hollowed has stood in the same stairway longer than my Vigil has had a Hall. We have decided it is waiting.

lines.text: A Hollowed's bones are the bones of someone we knew, the Remembrancers say. I will not carve them. Not for love, nor for a promise to say the names after.
We train for the Hollowed though we avoid them. It is for the moment one walks into the lane. It has never happened. We train as one practises a sentence one hopes never to say.
I keep a lantern at the lane's far edge, facing the fortresses. It is not for the Hollowed. It is for any Withren left in them who might remember the way home. It has never been touched.
Wart grows near the fortresses too. The soul sand there is old and tired, and the wart comes up pale. I do not eat it. I think of it as speaking in a whisper.
I mix a cup that would let a Hollowed rest, the old books say. It is a lie. Nothing lets them rest. But I pour the cup at the lane's edge anyway. It is a courtesy.
I carry no names for the Hollowed. They are not on the Wall, because they did not die. It is the great hole in my ledger. I would fill it if I knew how.
Parents tell children the Hollowed are the ones who never said goodbye. It is meant to make them say it. It works rather too well.

lines: I once saw a Hollowed stand at the edge of our lanterns' light. It looked at the flames. It did not step in. Perhaps something in it knew the rule. We left the lanterns burning, and it left.
Their skulls are the same as ours, if you look. Do not look long. You find yourself checking the jaw for a family likeness.

lines.text: We do not go to the fortresses. It is not fear. It is a debt we have not worked out how to pay, and walking in with empty hands would make it larger.
Have you stood among them in a fortress, outsider?

replies.text: Then you walked the houses of the dead with a blade. I do not ask you to apologise. I ask you to remember it.
Good. Do not go for treasure. If you must go, go with your head bowed and your hands slow.
*a long pause* Which name? No. Do not tell me. It was theirs. I thank you for it.

lines.text: The old growers say a brew might mend a Hollowed. The Brewers say it is not a brew's work. Which of them do you think is right?

replies.text: We have tried for longer than you have been alive. We shall try again when we have a new idea.
That is what everyone says. Nobody can tell us how to give rest to someone who is not there to receive it.

lines: Your people set three Hollowed skulls on soul sand. The Hollowed have no willing souls left. So what wakes has nothing in it that wants to stop.
Ours chose. Yours are woken. That is the whole difference, and it is a large one. Ours burned out. Yours have to be killed.

lines.text: Outsiders make Withers for a star and a shout. I have heard them call it a test of strength. Is it?

replies.text: Then they test it on three of our dead. I hope they pass. I hope they do not try again.
Yes. Thank you for saying it first. I did not want to.
*very quietly* Sport. I will write that on the Wall, beside the three it was done to.

lines: When you kill one, it leaves a star: three souls fused, all that is left of them. Bring it to the Hall of the Three. We will lay it with the ones who chose.
We know where you come from. We see it in your step. We do not hold it against you. We do watch your hands.
We know little of your world. We know it has a sky, and that the sky is not on fire. Tell me of it, if you wish. I do not stop listening easily.
Outsiders come through the burning gates one at a time, always frightened and always loud. We leave a lantern near the gate. It helps the loud ones calm down.
Your people use the Wither's star for lights on pillars. A beacon, you call it. I have seen one from far off. It is a beautiful light. I do not know what to do with that.
I do not hate you for the skulls. I hate the idea of the skulls. It is a distinction the Ashwardens do not always honour.

lines.text: If you ever feel the pull to try it, come here first. Sit by a lantern. Say three names. If the urge remains, tell me what it is made of. I would truly like to know.

lines: Outsiders are the only creatures that make the Wither on purpose. The ghasts do not. The Piglins do not. Even the blazes, who are not kind, do not. Think on that, when you feel proud.

lines.text: I keep a page in my ledger for outsiders who stayed for a Saying. It is the shortest page in the book. I cross none of them out. In a way they have all come back.
We let outsiders pass if they walk like they are lost. Those who walk like they are hunting get a longer look. Those who walk like they carry skulls get the longest.
An outsider once relit a lantern I had let burn low. They did not ask. They simply did it, and went on. I have thought of it for years. I would like to find them.
Outsiders take wart for brewing, too. We do not mind. We mind that they never thank the terrace. A terrace is somebody's life's work.
Outsiders brew with wart. I have heard of potions of strength, of speed, of leaping. Where is the potion of listening? You have had wart for ages and never once made that.
Out here I meet outsiders more than Withren. Most are polite. A few are armed. One tried to pay me in gold. I said we do not trade in things that remember nothing. They looked at it for a long time.
In {village} the children follow outsiders in a line, at a respectful distance, copying how they walk. If you notice, do not mention it. It is the highest compliment we have.
I think you are a fair example of your kind. I will say so to the others. They will not believe me. They will watch you more kindly anyway.
You are the first of your kind I have spoken with at such length. I will write it down, in case you are also the last.
What would your people say if they knew what you were doing here?

replies.text: Understanding takes time and a good bench. I hope you carry some of this home with you.
Curiosity is a good start. Add reverence and you will have a Withren.

replies.ask: They do not need to know.
replies.text: A secret kept from your own people is a small Wall. Do not let it grow.

lines.text: Would your people ever stop making them?

replies.text: Then they are the ones I should be speaking with. Send them. I will pour them something warm.
*a long, slow breath* Then we will keep the Hall open, and wait for you to be ashamed.

replies.ask: I will tell them not to.
replies.text: Thank you. Tell them with a lantern in your hand. A lantern makes words listen.

lines: The Piglins wanted the gold under our valleys. We would not let them dig through our dead to reach it. That was the War of the Hoard, in one breath.
They wear gold so they know each other in a fight, because nobody else would wear it. We never would. Gold remembers nothing.

lines.text: They blame us for the bastions. We blame them for the War. The Wither sits between us like a table nobody will eat at.

replies.text: Yes. Everyone lost. We lost first and last. Do not tell a Piglin I agreed with you.
They did. We finished it. I am not sure which is worse. The Wall does not say.
For outsiders in gold, perhaps. Go and wear it somewhere else.

lines: When a Piglin dies, nobody keeps them. They spend names like nuggets. I find that the saddest thing about them, and it has competition.

lines.text: If you smell of gold, stand downwind. I do not mean it as an insult. I mean it as geography.

lines: A Piglin once sat at the end of our lane for a very long stretch, glaring at the Hall and holding a gold ingot. We left a bench. They left a small carving of a hoglin. I still do not know why.
Piglins count everything. I respect it. Counting is a kind of remembering, so long as you do not spend what you count.
I do not hate the Piglins. It is hard to hate anyone with so many opinions. Hatred is quiet. They are never quiet.

lines.text: A Piglin once asked me to write their name down so it would last. I wrote it in ash on their wrist. They wore it until it faded, then asked again. I think that is their nearest thing to a Wall.

lines: They are brave in a way we are not. They shout their courage and we whisper ours. I have never decided which is the braver.
The Brutes are the saddest of them. Bred to guard what they cannot spend. We feel some kinship with that. We have not told them.

lines.text: I entered one Piglin in the ledger, a trader who died at our lane's end, unkept, with a nugget in the hand. I put the nugget in the margin. It seemed rude not to.
We stop Piglins at the lane's edge and ask them to take off their gold. Most refuse. We stop them anyway. Some walk away. Some come back without it. Those we call guests.
Piglins never light lanterns. They stoke fires. A fire says here we are. A lantern says here someone was. I tried to explain the difference to a Piglin. They gave me a coin.
Piglins carve tusks. I have seen their work. It is rough and bold and full of teeth. I would not copy it. I would, privately, like to have made it.
A Piglin once offered me a sack of gold for a flask against fire. I gave them the flask and returned the gold. They took it back with enormous suspicion.
On the roads you hear Piglins long before you see them. They are loud even at a distance, which is a courtesy. You always know when to stand aside.
{village} has never been raided by Piglins. Not once. We believe it is because they cannot find us. We believe we are also lucky. We do not discuss it.

lines: They believe your world rots you. They fear it. It strikes me as odd, in a people who walk a valley full of souls, to be called the strange ones.

lines.text: Have you made friends with a Piglin?

replies.text: Good. Perhaps you will tell them, some time, that someone here remembers their dead. They will not believe it. Tell them anyway.

replies.ask: No. They try to kill me.
replies.text: They do that. It is not personal. It is only gold.
Careful. They count everything, and they count the counting.

lines.text: If a Piglin came to the Hall, bareheaded and asking, what would you want us to do?

replies.text: We would. We would give them a bench. We would not give them the plinths. It is not yet that kind of peace.
Perhaps. But a door that never opens is only a wall.
We do not ask for kneeling. We ask for quiet. They would find that harder.

lines: The Magmari ferried the Piglin war-bands over the lava, for pay. Every Piglin that reached our valleys came on a Magmari barge.
The Last Answer burned their Moorings for it. They have not forgiven us. We have not forgiven the ferries. It is a very well-kept grudge, on both sides.
Warm, they call themselves. Friendly. Always cold, always haggling. I have never seen one sell a grudge, though. Those they keep.
A Magmari once told me they would ferry anything, for the right price. I asked the price of a dead name. They had no answer. I keep that too.
A Magmari dimmed at the Hall door once, out of respect. They glow when they are happy, and it went out like a candle. It was the finest manners I have seen from anyone.
They bring us nothing and ask for nothing. That is a real kindness, considering what they usually do, which is haggle until you give them whatever they like.
The Magmari say a debt unpaid is a debt kept warm. We say a debt unpaid is a name unspoken. Between those two sayings sits the whole of our quarrel.
I stood on a Mooring chain once. It hummed. I asked what it sang. They said, every maker of every link since it began. They keep names in iron. We keep ours in ash. It is the same habit.
Their striders are better kept than most of our Cairnbacks. I say this quietly. The Cairnbacks cannot hear, but I would not like them to overhear.

lines.text: I have a friend among the Magmari. I will not say who or where. It would complicate the friendship, and the grudge. I carry both. They are the same weight, oddly.

lines: The burning of the Moorings is in our account, in the same hand as the burning of our fortresses. We did not write it smaller. It is a small honour we gave them.

lines.text: I sent word to a Mooring asking the names of their dead from the burning. They returned a length of chain with the names stamped on the links. I keep it in the ledger. It is heavy. It is meant to be.
Ferries come near the valley edge sometimes. We do not stop them. We only watch, with spears lowered. Each side knows what the other is remembering.
A Magmari glows brighter than any lantern I tend, and a great deal more loudly. I am a little jealous. I am also a little glad not to be so warm.
A Magmari offered me lava-warmed soil for my terraces. It would grow wart like a fever. I declined. It would not be wart any more. It would be an opinion.
Their chains are iron, and iron is honest. It does not break, so it never ends up in a pocket as a keepsake. Bone breaks, and so it can be shared. I do not know which is better.
A Magmari bought a thimble of my fire-warding brew and paid with three links of chain. I wear them under my cloak, to remember that trade can be a truce.
No Magmari has ever set foot in {village}. They walk the lava and we walk the soul sand, and there is a good deal of ground between that neither of us wishes to cross.
At the edge of the lava sea I once waved at a ferry. The ferry waved back, and then thought better of it. We have not discussed it.
You travel with them? Then ask the name of the first Mooring burned. We have it written. I wonder whether they do.
Would you carry a message to a Mooring for me?

replies.text: Tell them the names of their burned ones are on our Wall, in the smallest letters we have. Do not say I sent it. Say someone did.
That their dead are kept somewhere. It is not enough. It is not nothing.
No. It is not. It is a pity how many things are no one's business.

lines.text: Do you think they will ever forgive us?

replies.text: In time. The Wall says time forgives nothing, but people do. I am comforted, and a little afraid.
No. We have not forgiven them either. It would be poor manners to hurry.

lines: In the War, the Weft walked the fields afterwards and took bone from the dead of both sides. Needles. Loom weights. Our dead are in their cloth, holding it down.
They weave their history, one row a year, and they put the Wither in as sixty black rows. Sixty. As if it were their grief to weave.

lines.text: A Weft once offered to weave my keeping into their Long Cloth. As a kindness. With what needle, I asked.

replies.text: It is. They did not see it. That is the horrible part. Four arms, and not one of them knows when to stop.
Perhaps they did. Meaning well is cheap. Bone is not.
Then give them yours. *a pause* No? Then it is not only bone.

lines: Our bone comes from the valley, from beasts nobody kept. Theirs came from people with names. That is the difference. They do not think there is one.
A Weft once showed me a needle and told me, with great pride, how fine it was. I asked where the bone came from. They said, from a battlefield. They did not see why I left.
They click their mandibles when they think. I find it unsettling. It sounds like a Hollowed counting. I told them so. They clicked. I could not tell whether it was an apology.
They are not wicked. That is the trouble. A wicked people would be easier to forgive. The Weft only did not see what they took. They were making something beautiful, and it needed weighting.
In their cloth a thread runs through every row, the warp-line. It is the forest. We have no cloth. We have a Wall. A Wall cannot be threaded, only read.
Four arms. I have watched one letter a name, tie a knot, hold a lantern and eat, all together. I would find it very tiring to be so useful.

lines.text: A Weft sent me a small cloth woven with the first half of my name. They did not weave the second. They said they could not weave what they could not see. I was moved, which I show by being very still.

lines: We do not trade with the Weft, and we do not fight them. They are too busy being sure they are right to start a fight. It leaves a great deal of peace.
A Weft apologised to me once, for the bone. It was a good apology. I told them it was good. It changed nothing, but I thought they should know.

lines.text: I have read the sixty black rows. I was permitted a visit, with a guide. They are woven with such care. I found it very hard to hate the hand that made them.
I am told the Weft string nets for Ghastkin elsewhere. We do not help them. We also do not cut the nets. It is an honest cowardice. I am working on it.
The Weft light their halls with shroomlight, warm yellow. Ours is blue. I stood in one once, and my lantern looked pale and embarrassed.
A Weft Dyer once asked me for wart for a blue dye. I said no, then yes, then no. We have a long and confusing history with each other.
I would carve a needle for any Weft who asked, from valley bone, from beasts nobody kept. They have never asked. I think they prefer the old kind. I think they do not know what the old kind is.
The Weft drink a fungus tea that makes them very precise. I tried a cup. I was precise for a long while. I still know the exact number of sips I took. It was nine.
Our children are told the Weft are not to be trusted with bone. Our children ask what they may be trusted with. The answer is thread. It is a small consolation prize.
In the wild I have met Weft travelling with cloth. They bow with all four arms at once. It is the politest greeting I have ever had, and I do not trust it.
A Weft once asked why we keep names of people we never met. I asked why they weave rows of years they never lived. They clicked for a long while. Then they said, oh.

replies.text: A small one, but a sharp one. I do not make many.
Perhaps. Said gently, a grudge sounds like a friendship. I am not ready to hear it yet.

lines.text: Do you think the Weft could ever make it right?

replies.text: They could. Some say they have begun. I will believe it when I see a needle made of wood. And I will mourn how long it took.

replies.ask: They could weave your dead in.
replies.text: They did. That is the grievance. They did, and thought it a kindness.
Forgetting is not ours to give, outsider. We keep what we are given, including grudges.

lines: The Ghastkin cry once for each death, and the tears wash the memory away. They call it letting go. We call it a second death, done gently.
We keep every name. They cry names away. You can see why we do not share a valley.
Half of them swelled into ghasts, grieving the Last Answer. That is our grief, floating overhead, still crying. I do not know what to say to it. I keep its silence.

lines.text: A Ghastkin once offered to cry for {kept}, so I could rest. I said no. They said I looked tired. I did. I said no.

replies.text: I think so. It would have been easier to be wrong. Easier things often are.
I rest. I rest with the name in my mouth. It is the only way we know.
*a cold look* That is the one thing you must never say in a Vigil. I will pretend you did not.

lines: Their tears close wounds. I have an old scar they could close. I keep it. It is where I stood when I first learned {kept}'s name. A scar is a kind of keeping too.
A Ghastkin told me their name, and a year later told me another. I said, you have changed. They said, I have healed. We each thought the other was missing something.
They say grief has a shape, that it is round and floats. I find that lovely and I find it unbearable. I would not give up either feeling.
Their Weeping Hall holds the only water in the Nether, I am told. We have none. We have ash, and a Wall. I never wanted water. I wanted the permission.

lines.text: If I am honest, and with you I may be, I have wondered what it would be like to forget something. Once, gently. I would take it back the next moment. I would only like to know.

lines: I count the ghasts overhead when I walk the valley. One for each name I know was lost to the Last Answer. I never reach the end.
A Ghastkin child cannot cry yet. Their eyes stay open. They look at the Wall as if it were written in a language they hope never to read. I find I stand straighter.

lines.text: I keep a column in my ledger for names the Ghastkin have let go. I write them in the smallest hand. It is not judgement. It is hospitality. Someone should hold what they set down.
Ghastkin drift near our edge sometimes. We do not turn them away. We ask, politely, that they not cry on the lanterns. A lantern lit for a name dislikes being told to forget.
A Ghastkin tear fell on one of my lanterns once. The flame hissed and went white. I have not decided whether it was dimmed or freed. I relit it, of course.
A Ghastkin asked me to carve a small bone vessel to hold a tear. I did. They filled it and gave it back. It sits on my bench. I do not know what it is for. I do not touch it.
I know a brew that steadies a grief, a brew that dulls it, and a Ghastkin brew that removes it. The third is theirs and I have not made it. I mention it in case you wondered.
{village} lies under two ghasts that keep drifting back. We have named them. I will not say what. It would be unkind to say it aloud near them.
Once in the valley a Ghastkin sat down beside me, and said nothing, and I said nothing, and we stayed a long while. It was the best conversation I had that year.
I do not dislike them. I disagree with them. There is a large room between those two, and I live in it.
If a Ghastkin wept for me when I die, I would not mind. I would only want someone to keep my name afterwards. The two together might be enough.
If a Ghastkin offered to cry for someone you had lost, what would you say?

replies.text: It might. I do not know that I want it eased. I want it carried. Those are different loads.
Yes. That is the answer. I did not expect it of an outsider. Thank you.
It is. I cannot deny it. I only wish it did not take the name along with the pain.

lines.text: Do you suppose we are right and they are wrong? Or the other way about?

replies.text: That is the answer I most dislike, because it is the likeliest. Thank you for it.
Thank you. I will try not to enjoy it.
*a long silence* Perhaps in some ways. I cannot say so near the Wall. I will say it here, quietly, to you.

lines: Nether wart grows only on soul sand. The old growers said it drinks the patience of the dead. It certainly drinks ours.
Soul fire burns blue because it burns on soul sand and soul soil. We light our lanterns from it. It is the only fire here that wants nothing.
Every brew begins with wart. You cannot make anything good without first making something awkward. That is true of brewing, and of visits.
The first brew from each terrace goes to the Hall. The Three do not drink it. Nobody else may either. That is how you know it is a gift.
Wart ripens in four stages: nub, leaf, knot and crown. The crown is red as an ember, and we harvest at the crown. Late wart is bitter and cross.
Soul fire does not spread. It sits on its fuel and keeps still. We trust it more than any other fire for that reason. Ordinary fire wants to go places.
Every Vigil keeps four brews: Mending, Fireward, Steadying and Returning. Steadying is the warm one. Returning is thin and bitter, and we pour it after the Saying.
Wart grows on soul sand and nowhere else. Soul soil it merely tolerates, like a polite guest. The growers can tell at a glance which terraces are old sand and which are borrowed.
Blaze powder is the quickest heat for a brew, and we use it sparingly. It is fire taken from something that was still angry. Slow fire from the lanterns tastes better and sits easier.

lines.text: Here is the oldest brewers' rule, and it is not written: never brew when you are angry. The pot remembers. I have thrown out batches that tasted of an argument.

lines: Glass bottles are precious here. We wash and keep every one. A bottle can outlast the person who first filled it. Several in the brewery are older than the Hall.

lines.text: On long watches an Ashwarden may carry a flask of Steadying. It does nothing but warm the hands. I have found that a thing which does nothing is the best thing to drink on duty.
Soul fire is the only light that never gets into the eyes. A steady blue, it sits where you put it. I think that is why we love it. It is not trying to wake anyone.
I can tell the age of a terrace by the sound a spade makes in it. Young sand sings high. Old sand answers low, like someone turning over. I have never found a terrace that did not answer.
I carve the stirring bones for the brewery, long and smooth, one for each pot. They wear down in a lifetime. Then I carve the next. Every stirring bone has a name scratched in it.
My first batch tasted of burnt wood and apology. I served it to the Remembrancer, who drank every drop and said it was a start. I have never forgotten how kind that was.
There is a seat by the brewery fire, and it belongs to whoever is grieving most. They need not speak. They need only stir. The pot always seems to know.
The brewery in {village} smells of wart, smoke and ash. We call the smell Home. It is the first thing a child notices when they come back from the lane.
I carry a small flask of wart brew out here, and a little soul fire in a bottle. Neither is much. Together they are almost a hearth. They are at least a reason.
You are welcome to a cup, if you wish. Warm, bitter, honest. It does nothing to the mind and a great deal to the hands.
Do you want to know the secret of a good brew?

replies.text: Attention. That is all. Hold the pot and mean it. Wart knows when you are thinking about something else.
Neither are most who drink it. But anyone can pay attention to a pot. Try it once. It is a lesson in humility.

lines.text: Do you think fire has a memory?

replies.text: Soul fire burns on what the dead left behind. I think it has a little. I think it has more than we care to hear.
Perhaps is a good answer here. We say it often. It is very nearly a prayer.
That is a very practical sentence. I would not say it near a Cairnback.

lines.text: Not yet. A name has to be heavy enough to carry first. Yours is getting there. Come back. Bring it with you.
Outsiders are never on the Wall. You would be the first. I would have to ask the Remembrancer for a very long sign.
Yes. When you die, I will keep your name. One keeping each is the rule. I asked {kept}. They do not mind sharing.
You are Kept. I will say your name when I rise, when I eat and when I lie down. You will not be finished while I am here.

replies.text: Do not thank me. Live a long while. It is easier to keep someone with a lot of stories.
Then you go on the Wall beside me, and a child chooses us both. They will have two to carry. They will manage.

lines.text: You ask as if it were a favour. It is not a favour. It is a weight, and I will weigh it before I agree to carry it.
There is a form of words, and I am not yet permitted to say it to you. I may tell you it is short. The short ones are always the hardest.
I have started a page for you in my head. Not a sign, yet. A page, with a few lines. Please take care what you do next. I would like to write more of the good parts.
I asked {kept}, as much as one can ask. They did not object. That is how the dead approve.
Most outsiders want to be remembered for what they did. I would keep you for how you listened. It is rarer, and it is harder to carve.
I have scratched your name inside the hem of my cloak, where nobody looks. It is not tidy, and it is not official, and it is mine.
Being kept is not one-sided. If I carry you, you must carry me a little too. Say my name once, when you are far away. It will do.
If you asked me, I would put you in the ledger of waiting names. You would be the first with a pulse. I would have to find a new column.
Only children hang lanterns on bone hooks, lit for the living, until they choose. I have one bone hook left over. I have been saving it for someone. Do not ask who.
I would brew for you. Nothing to forget with. A hot, dull one, to drink while talking. I would leave it bitter, because you strike me as someone who can take it.
Tell me something dull about yourself. The dull parts are what a keeping is made of.

replies.text: Good. A hum is worth keeping. I will remember it when I am the only one who still can.
Everyone says that. Everyone has a dull habit with a hum in it. Look for yours.
Then you are not ready to be kept. It is no shame. A name that cannot be told cannot be carried.

lines.text: What would you want said when your name is spoken? Not the deeds. One sentence. We choose it for the Saying, and most take years.

replies.text: A good sentence, but a crowded one. Many are kind. Try something only you could have said.
Short, and true, and it will outlast longer ones. The Wall has many such. They read best.
Nobody does. Carry the question about with you. A question is a very good thing to be kept for.

lines: A Cairnback carries a soul fire on its back that does not go out while it lives. We walk them at the head of every Vigil, so the dead can see the way.
They are slow. That is the point. Nobody hurries a procession, and nobody hurries a Cairnback. It saves a great many arguments.
Hold a torch to its shell and the torch comes away burning blue. Every lantern in the Vigil was lit that way. The Cairnback does not mind.

lines.text: When a Cairnback dies, its fire goes out with it. We keep their names too. Someone has to.

replies.text: Of course. {neighbour} keeps the name of the old one, before this one. It was called Patience. It was not.
So is everything, eventually. Then it is a name, and then it is only a name if nobody keeps it.

lines: A Cairnback's back is stacked like a cairn, which is where the name comes from. Each layer is a year of its life. Count them, if it lets you.
A Cairnback will not walk a lane whose lanterns have gone out. Nobody has got one past the first dark post. The Lantern-keepers say it is good taste. The Ashwardens say it is good sense.
We feed them wart stalks and the husks of brews, and they eat as if apologising. Each mouthful takes a long time. One watches, and one's own hurry begins to look ridiculous.
Every child is held up beside a Cairnback in their first year, so the fire will know them. The Cairnback does not mind. It does not notice. It is a mild start to being ignored by something kind.
A Cairnback's fire dims when it is unwell. It brightens when it is content, which is rarely, and only for a moment. We call that moment a blessing and try not to ask for another.

lines.text: The old Cairnback at the lane's end was my first friend. It stood beside me through three of my worst years and said nothing, and that was exactly the right amount.

lines: They do not lie down, as far as anyone knows. They stand so completely that you forget they are alive. Then one blinks, and the whole lane breathes in.

lines.text: I keep the Cairnbacks' names in the ledger, beside the people's. Some think it odd. It is a ledger of who was here, and they were here. They were slow about it, but they were here.
On watch a Cairnback is better company than any of us. It does not talk, it does not shift, and it never claims it saw something. When it does look up, I look too.
My lanterns are lit from the Cairnback by hand, a torch at a time. I hold the torch to the shell and say thank you. It does not answer, but the flame goes steady.
I plant a row just for the Cairnbacks at the terrace edge. They eat the first stalks and leave the roots. I take that as an agreement, though neither of us signed.
I polish my carvings with flakes a Cairnback's shell has shed. They give a warm sheen. I never take one the animal has not already let go.
A Cairnback can smell a good brew from the end of the lane. They stand at the brewery door and sigh. I give them the dregs. It is the one verdict I trust.
In {village} the Cairnbacks have their own lane, wide, with none of our lanterns. Their own fires light it. They seem to prefer that. It looks like a river of small hearths.
A wild Cairnback once followed me the whole long way across the valley. I called it a companion. It called me nothing. I think it had a better idea of the distance than I.
You may walk behind one in a procession, if you keep a polite distance. It is an honour, and a test. You will want to pass it. Do not.

lines: A Cairnback's fire has never set anything alight that it was not asked to. We have tested this carelessly, many times, by accident.

lines.text: Would you like to meet the oldest Cairnback in our Vigil?

replies.text: It is by the Hall. Do not hurry toward it. It takes its time with strangers, and it will take it with you.
As safe as a candle in good hands. Do not push the shell. Do not feed it gold. It knows.

lines.text: Do you think they know what the fire is for?

replies.text: That is the kind way to say it. I like it. I will tell it to the next child.
Then say that to the one carrying it. Slowly. In the Hall.
Perhaps. We have never asked. Asking seems exactly the kind of thing they would not mind and not answer.

lines: I do not know yet! At my first Vigil I walk the Name Wall and choose. I keep changing my mind. There are so many, and they all look lonely.
{neighbour} says to choose someone with a short name, so it is easy to say. I think that is lazy. I want a long one. I want it to be work.

lines.text: Who would you choose, if you were me? Someone brave, or someone nobody else has chosen?

replies.text: That is what I think too! Then they have somebody. Then they are not only a sign.
Brave ones get chosen a lot. I might still. I will think very hard about it. *frowns very hard*
It is not silly! It is the most important thing I will ever do. You are not invited to my Vigil.

lines: Sometimes I practise. I pick a name off the Wall and say it all the way home. Then I feel bad for putting it back.
I am supposed to walk the Wall at least three times before I choose. Three is the custom. I have walked it twice. I am saving the third for when I am braver.
Some signs have a little hole where a lantern hook used to be. I like those ones. It means somebody used to care a lot.
There is a very short name by the door, from a very short life. Nobody has chosen it. I stop there every time. I do not know if that is choosing.
My parent keeps someone brave and {neighbour} keeps someone clever. I want to keep someone who was good at waiting. Waiting is what we do the most. We should have a name for it.
The Bonecarver is already making my toggle, before I choose. It is blank. They said blank is a promise. I think blank is nervous.

lines.text: I do not usually tell strangers about my choosing. But you look like someone who would keep a secret, or at least forget it politely.
You asked about my choosing twice. Most people only ask once. You must be a keeper of questions. I will keep that in mind.
If I choose someone brave, will I be brave? Or will I only be tired from trying? I ask you because you do things. Grown-ups only talk about them.

lines: I practise by picking a name from the Wall and being them for the length of the lane. Last time I was a Lantern-keeper. I tripped. It was very realistic.
