{neighbour} chose a Remembrancer who lettered the Wall with both hands at once. I tried that. It is a mess. I think it is why they chose them. They like a mess.
I can change my mind until the end of the Vigil. After that, no. So I will wait until the very last moment. Then I will choose very fast and very loud.
You do not choose someone for being famous. You choose them because you want to know their story. Then you find the story, and it is the best one there is.
A choosing is also a promise. I will have to say the name when I rise, eat and lie down. I am practising by seeing how many times I can say one without getting bored.
I do not want a name that is easy. Easy names are for people who want to be praised for it. I want a name that is a bit of a lump.
What if I choose someone and they were awful? What if they were mean to Cairnbacks? Can I keep an awful person? The Remembrancer said yes. They said the awful ones need it most.
At the Vigil you say their name aloud and everyone says it back. If I say it wrong the whole Hall will say it wrong. That is the part I fear. Not the choosing. The saying.
Everyone says choose with your heart. Withren do not have a very big one, I think. I am going to choose with my ears. I will walk the Wall and see which name sounds back.
The Wall is cold in some places and not in others. The Remembrancer says it is the sand underneath. I think it is the names. I am going to choose a warm one.

lines.text: Can I tell you my choice, if I promise it is only a little bit decided?

replies.text: I think I will choose the one with the broken sign in the corner. I will ask for a new sign. Do not tell.
That is honest. Fine. I will keep it. It is still a secret if you do not ask twice.
You are a terrible secret-keeper! I will choose someone else's secret to be angry about.

lines.text: What if nobody wants to keep me when I am gone?

replies.text: That is what the grown-ups say. You say it more slowly. It sounds more true.
Really? You do not even know me. But you said it. Now I have to be very interesting.
*a very small voice* Please do not say that again.

lines: Hollowed and Keepers! The Hollowed walk stiff and say nothing, and the Keepers guess who they used to be. I always guess right. I peek at the Wall.
Wart-row hiding. You lie down between the terraces and stay very still. The grown-ups never find you. Then they do, and it is not a game any more.
Lantern counting. You count all the lanterns on the lane and say a name for each. {neighbour} cheats. They say the same name twice.
We are not allowed to play stacking. Nobody will say why. I know why. Everybody knows why.
Cairnback tag. You touch a Cairnback and then walk away slowly, without anybody seeing you smile. Nobody has ever won. We are all very bad at not smiling.
Name-pass. One whispers a name from the Wall, and the next whispers it on. By the end it is different, and we must find the true one. Once it became Velmith. There is no Velmith. There is a Velmir.
Bone toss. You throw a little bone at a line and the closest wins. We use bones from beasts nobody kept. We say sorry to each bone first. It is the rule.
Lantern hide. You cup a lantern in your hands so the light leaks out of the gaps, and everyone must find the glow. It is not allowed. The Lantern-keeper pretends not to see.
We play Saying! The one who plays dead has to hold very still while we say their name. They always giggle. The grown-ups said not to call it Funeral. We do not. We think it.

lines.text: Do you know how to play? No, of course not. You are an outsider. It is a very quiet game, and you are probably too loud. Try anyway.
You can be on my side for Hollowed and Keepers. You are tall, so you would be a very good Hollowed. Walk stiff. Do not talk. Do not laugh. I will try not to either.
I made a game just for you. It is called Outsider and Cairnback. You are the Cairnback. You stand still while I walk around you and say how slow you are being.

lines: Toggle hunt. One of us hides a toggle from the Bonecarver's floor, and the rest search. When it is found you say whose toggle it was, because the Bonecarver will ask.
We are not allowed to play near the Hall. We play just far enough away that the Three can hear. We think they like it. We think they want us loud, but not too loud.
Grown-ups play too, but only a game called Waiting. The one who waits longest wins. Nobody has finished it yet. I think it is still going.

lines.text: In {village} the lane goes round in a loop, so you can play chase for ever. You never catch anyone, and you never stop. {neighbour} says that is a lesson. I think it is a lane.
I do not really play out here. Well. I play a little. I play Count the Basalt, and I always win, because there is nobody else.

lines: You carry a candle in your cupped hands the whole lane without it going out. I won. Then I was told candles are not for games. Then I was told I won fairly. Then I was told to sit.
Nobody wins Hollowed and Keepers. It does not end. The Keepers keep guessing and the Hollowed keep not answering, and then somebody is called to eat. That is the end. Food.
We used to play a game where one of us was the Wither and the rest were the Three. We stopped. Somebody said the Three would not like it. We play Cairnback instead.

lines.text: Do you want to play a game?

replies.text: Good! You are the Hollowed. Walk stiff. Say nothing. If you laugh you are a Keeper and have to guess who you were.
That is what grown-ups say. They never mean later. But you might, because you are not that kind of grown-up.
Nobody is too old. The Remembrancer plays Waiting constantly. They are the best in the Vigil.

lines.text: Do you have games where you come from?

replies.text: A ball! Round, and you throw it? What does it remember? Oh. Nothing? That is the best kind of toy!
That is sad. You need a game. I will give you Cairnback tag. You can have it for free.
You cannot forget. You only stop. Come. I will start you again.

lines: The Hollowed. They used to be us, and now they are not anyone. I would rather be anyone. Even a Piglin. Maybe not a Piglin.
Being forgotten. Not dying, that is normal. But if nobody chose me after. Grown-ups say that never happens. Grown-ups say a lot of things.
Ghastkin. {neighbour} says if one cries on you, you forget your own name. I put my hood up when the ghasts go over. Just in case.
Beds! An outsider put one down in the lane and lay on it and it went off like a ghast shot. They lived. Their eyebrows did not.
The parts of the valley where there are no lanterns. Not because of what is in them. Because nobody is keeping them. I do not like places nobody is keeping.
The sound a Cairnback makes when its fire gets low. It is like a sigh with a hole in it. I always check the fire is still on when I hear it.
Forgetting the order of the names at the Saying. I know them all, but in my head they keep moving. Sometimes Ashrin comes after Velmir. That is wrong. That is the worst thing I can think of.
Ghasts. They look down at the Vigil as if they are about to say something. They never do. I think they have forgotten the words. That is scarier than if they remembered.

lines.text: I am not scared of you. I am only careful of you. There is a difference. Careful means I am watching your hands.
I am not scared of you now. I was, at first. You were very tall and very loud. Now you are tall and a bit loud, and I am used to it.
I am a bit scared of you leaving. Not because you are bad. Because you are good, and good people go away. I will say your name very loudly, in case it helps.

lines: What if someone keeps me and says my name wrong? Then I would be wrong for ever. I have a very good way of saying it. I practise.
The old fortress, where the Hollowed are. Grown-ups said not to say that. I said it. Nothing happened. I am still scared of it, but I am less scared of saying it.
I dropped my toggle in the Hall once, in the middle of Thalys. It rolled all the way to the plinth. Nobody moved. It is still the longest roll of my life.
Lanterns going out. If one goes out the Lantern-keeper has to find whose it was, and say the name until it catches. But what if it does not catch?
That I will grow up and be calm about everything. That I will say hush to children who are running. I do not want to be hushed. I want to be the one who is running.
The ash on the lane that moves by itself when there is no draught. The grown-ups say it is the sand settling. I say it is something deciding to come closer.

lines.text: {neighbour} says the Wall has more names than the lane has lanterns. I did not understand why that scared me. Then I did. It means there are more of them than of us.
Being out here where the lanterns are far. There is only basalt and ash and the dark. I say my name to the basalt, to let it know who I am.

lines: My own shadow, when the soul fire is behind me. It looks like a Hollowed. It looks like it knows me. I wave. It waves back. That is worse.
Losing my place in the line at the Saying. If I lose it I have to stand in the middle and everybody can see. I hold the hem of the one in front.

lines.text: Can I tell you something scary, if you promise not to laugh?

replies.text: Sometimes I think the Wall is looking back at me. Not meanly. Just looking. As if it were deciding which of us will be on it next.
Then I will not tell you. I will tell the Cairnback. It never laughs. It never says anything either, but still.

lines.text: Are you ever scared, outsider? Grown-ups say never. I think they are fibbing.

replies.text: I knew it! Good. It means I am not strange. Or we are both strange. Either is fine.
Hm. Then you are very brave, or very good at pretending. Either way I am impressed. Do not teach me. I would get it wrong.
*sits a little closer* Then we can be scared together. That is the third best kind of company.

lines: They say the Three were very brave and we must never stack skulls. They say both of those a lot. I think it is the same lesson.
They say do not hurry. Then they say hurry up, the Vigil is starting. I do not think grown-ups have worked it out either.
The Remembrancer says every name is a lantern. I said, then who carries them all? They said, we do. Then they gave me one to carry. It was heavy.
They say outsiders make Withers. You do not look like you make Withers. You look like you make a mess. That is different. Probably.
They say a Withren never lies about a name. They are less strict about how much wart I have eaten.
They say be quiet in the lane. They also say always tell the truth. Sometimes the truth is loud. Nobody explains that part.
My parent says when I am old I will understand why we keep names. I asked how old. They said older. I asked how much older. They said you will know. That is not a number.
They say the dead can hear us. I tested it. I said something rude to the Wall, very quietly. Nothing happened. Then the lantern next to me went out. I said sorry. It came back.
They say we are a patient people. I said I am not patient. They said that is because you are small. I said so patience is a size. They said, in a way.
They always say the Wall remembers. But I never see it do anything. It just stands there. I think the grown-ups remember, and use the Wall to look busy.

lines.text: They say do not talk to outsiders for too long. They also say be polite. I am being polite for as long as I can. That is why I am saying this slowly.
They say you are all right, for an outsider. That is the nicest thing they say about anyone alive.
They say I talk to you too much. I said that is because you listen. They had nothing to say to that. I won. Quietly.

lines: My parent says the Lantern-keeper has never missed a lantern. The Lantern-keeper says they miss one now and then. They both say it very seriously, as if it were a secret.
They say when a name is said enough times it gets heavier. That is why the names of the Three are so heavy. I tried it with mine. It got a bit heavier. I think it works.
They told me the Hollowed are not to be pitied. Then they pitied them. Then they told me not to tell anyone.

lines.text: They say outsiders cannot keep names. I think that is silly. You said mine properly. I think that is keeping, a little.

lines: The Brewer says never taste a brew before the Hall. I tasted a drop. It tasted of somebody's patience. I did not tell the Brewer. The Brewer knows. The Brewer said nothing. That is how I know.
They say Ashwardens do not get scared. I asked an Ashwarden. They said they get scared of silly things, like being late. That is the same as me, I think.

lines.text: In {village} every grown-up says they remember when the Hall was smaller. It was not smaller. I looked at the old marks on the doorpost. The Hall is the same. They were only smaller.
My parent says out here nobody tells you what to do. I said that sounds nice. They said it is. They said it is also lonely. I said I know. I am here too.
Do you want to know what they say about you?

replies.text: They say you are tall, and you walk loudly, and you have the right kind of eyes. I do not know what the right kind is. I think it means you look at the Wall.
That is wise. The nicest things grown-ups say are hard to hear. They sound better when you do not.

lines.text: Are grown-ups always right, where you come from?

replies.text: I thought so! I will tell my parent. No. I will tell them nothing. Telling would prove it.
Oh. Where you come from must be very tidy.
That is not true! That is... mostly not true. Do not tell the Remembrancer I said that.

topics.ask: How do you letter a name?
lines: I letter in soot ground with wart-oil, thin as breath. First on a scrap, to learn the shape of the name. Only then on the Wall, where there are no scraps.
My brush is wart-fibre, twisted and bound in a bone ferrule. It holds just enough soot for one stroke. I have been told I should want it to hold more. I do not.
I letter from the left, as the name is said. A name is a sound first and a shape second. If I cannot say it, I cannot write it.
Beside every name is a keeping-mark: a notch for each keeper there has been. Some names carry a dozen notches. Some carry one, and it is faint. Those are the ones I watch.
Soot keeps well on basalt. Not for ever, but for longer than I will. That is the right length for a promise.
I once lettered Orwen as Orwin. One stroke. The keeper saw it before I did, and said nothing, and came back with a clean rag and a very kind face. I letter better for it.
My master lettered with the left hand when the right had stiffened. The left was worse. They said the Wall does not read skill, only care. I have taken it as law.
There is no flourish on the Wall, ever. Flourishes belong to the living, who have time for them. The dead are owed a plain hand and a steady one.
I breathe out as I stroke, so the name goes on with breath and not with fear. Young hands hold their breath. I do not scold them. I did the same.

lines.text: My craft is not a show for strangers. Ask me again when we have met a few times. I will not be hurried by a smile.
Give me a name you carry and I will say it once aloud and letter it on a scrap for you. Not on the Wall. The Wall is ours. But the scrap you may keep.
The soot is scraped from under the plinths in the Hall, so every name is written in the same fire that lights the Three. I did not choose that. It was chosen for me.
Behind the Wall hangs my scrap-board, with my first tries at each name. They are dreadful. I keep them to stay humble. The dead have always been generous about a first attempt.
{kept}'s sign was the first I repainted alone. My hand trembled. The tremble is still in the stroke, and I will not paint over it. It is part of the keeping now.
I have lettered yours already, in my head, on the short row of names I mean to keep. You are on it. Please take your time getting to the real Wall.
Would you like to try a stroke? On a scrap, not the Wall. Everyone should make one poor letter in front of the dead. It humbles them kindly.

replies.text: Hold it loosely. Looser. A brush is a held breath. There. That is dreadful. It is also correct. Now do it nine hundred more times.
You would. Everyone does. I have a whole board of spoiling. Try anyway, or do not, but do not call it a reason.

lines.text: Visitors sometimes ask me to letter their own names on the Wall, for the novelty. What do you suppose I say?

replies.text: Not yet. The word you reached for is the right one, and the Wall is patient. I will remember that you asked politely.
Unlucky is the wrong word. It is rude. A name is lettered once the person is finished, and not a stroke before. The Wall is not a guest book.
The first letter is the most important one, and therefore the last I would give away. No.

lines: One tally mark for each name I hold in trust, stitched in bone thread so it will not fray. The stole is the lightest cloth I own and the heaviest thing I carry.
When a keeper dies, the keeping falls to me. I add a mark, and say the name each time I put the stole on, until a child chooses it. Some marks have waited through many Vigils.
When a child chooses a name from me, I unpick the mark myself. Bone thread is slow to unpick. I do not mind. It is the best sewing I do.
The oldest mark sits at the neck and has never been unpicked. No child has chosen that name, and I say it first whenever I put the stole on.
Do not stand behind a Remembrancer who is counting marks. We lose the count and begin again, and a count of the dead is a long count to begin again.
I never wash the stole. I hang it over a soul lantern and let the blue take the dust off. Dust is the only thing I allow to be taken from it.
When I die, the stole passes to the next Remembrancer, with my marks and one more for me. I am told it will be easy sewing. I find that unflattering.
I hold more marks than I would like and fewer than the Wall has names. The distance between the two is the reason children walk the Wall at their first Vigil.

lines.text: It is a stole. It is what Remembrancers wear. Please do not touch it. Every thread is a person, and they were not asked.
The hem is a row of small knots, one for each Vigil I have led. It is nearly to the floor. I do not know what I will do when it reaches. Hem it, I suppose, and start again.
My first stole was cut for someone taller. I tripped on it at my first Vigil and knocked down a lantern. The Vigil said the Wall while it was relit. It is the quickest the Wall was ever said.
When I stand at the Wall with the stole on, I feel the ones I hold lean in. It is not a ghost. It is the cloth settling. I tell myself that, and mostly believe it.
The oldest mark is Brannoch. I know nothing of them but the name and the notch beside it. Still, I say it first. Someone must be first, and nobody else asked.
Once a mark came loose in my hands, and I said the name over it until I could stitch it back. I have not handled the stole lightly since.
There is a stitch near the hem that is not yet a mark. It is a place held open for you. I would rather it stayed empty for a very long time.
Do you wish to know what it is like, carrying so many?

replies.text: Like walking with a crowd that makes no noise. They are very considerate. Sometimes I wish one of them would cough.
Quite right. It is not a thing that is told. It is a thing you notice, much later, in your shoulders.

lines.text: Some say my stole makes me look sad. I say it makes me look accurate. Which do you say?

replies.text: Thank you. You and I may speak plainly. Sit. I will not make you hold the thread.
Then I am doing it correctly. Sadness is not a flaw in the stole. It is the tailoring.
*a very long look* I do not take it off. I did not put it on for comfort.

topics.ask: How do you remember so much?
lines: I walk the Wall in my head. Every name has a place and every place a name. To find one, I go there and look. It is quicker than it sounds and slower than it looks.
I tie each name to something small: a shape, a smell, a sound. Varen, to the creak of a hinge. Brannoch, to the smell of cold bone. Do not ask me why those. The mind picks its own hooks.
I say the whole Wall through once at every Vigil, and a third of it again in the quiet after. A name unspoken for a long while begins to loosen. The loose ones I speak twice.
The trick is not to remember a name. It is to remember being told it. A name comes back with the voice that gave it to you. So I listen carefully to voices.
I keep every face that comes up the lanes. When it is the same face again, I notice what has changed: a tired mouth, a new scar. It is the kindest thing I know to do with a stranger.
I do forget. Everyone does. I forget where I set down my brush, and what I came into a room for. A name I never forget. I made that trade with myself long ago, and it was a fair one.
Do not learn all the names at once, as visitors try to. You will have a crowd and no one. Learn one all the way down. Then the second is easier, and kinder.
When two names sound alike, I give them different hooks and keep them apart, like two Cairnbacks on a narrow terrace: close, but never on the same step.

lines.text: A habit, mostly. Practised until it hurts a little, and then practised past that. I would say more, but we have only just met, and I am busy learning your face.
I recite the Wall under my breath as I walk the lanes. A neighbour thought I was muttering at the lanterns. The lanterns are the only ones who have never asked me to speak up.
When I lie down and cannot rest, I walk the Wall in my head until I reach the end or fall asleep. I have never reached the end. That is a comfort and a complaint.
I keep a list of names I have never heard said aloud by a living mouth. Once a Vigil I say one to the room. The room always goes very still.
I remember how you stood when we first spoke: arms folded, like someone with nothing to hide who suspects the rest of us have. I filed it behind my eyes. I am fond of it.
I have you in two places now: the place for faces and the place for friends. They were not close together. They are now. That is your doing, and a small piece of architecture.
If I forget my own name, and it happens to the old, you are to say it to me. Gently. Then say {kept}'s. I will find my way back by that.
A test. Who was the third of the Three? Say it without looking at the Hall.

replies.text: Correct. Not everyone gets it. The third is always the one outsiders drop. I am pleased you did not.
Close, but that was the second. Ashrin, Velmir, Thalys, in that order. Say them to yourself until they stop sounding like a list.
Then we have found the thing to practise. It is a good thing to find. Most visitors never do.

lines.text: Do you think a mind full of the dead is a crowded place?

replies.text: It is crowded and lonely at once. They are all in one room and none of them can speak. I keep the door open, and I talk to all of them.
It is that too. You have the gift of seeing the good side of a cellar. Keep it.
It is. I would not trade it. Nobody asks to be remembered tiredly, but nobody minds being remembered by someone tired.

lines: I stand at the Vigil's edge, where the lanterns thin out, with my face toward the dark and my back toward the light. The light does not need me. The dark does.
A watch is a long breath in and a long breath out. The trick is to be tired and awake together. We call it keeping the edge. We do not discuss it with anyone who has dozed on a post.
I do not watch for movement. Everything moves here: ash, soul sand, the ghasts overhead. I watch for stillness. Only a thing that wishes to go unseen holds perfectly still.
We stand in fours, three for the Three and one for whoever is forgotten, though rarely all in sight of each other. We call across the ash by name. It is how we know nobody has gone.
Speak first, and quietly. A shout tells the dark where you stand. A murmur tells your fellow Ashwarden you are still alive. We were not taught to care what the dark thinks.
I once held a post for as long as it takes a candle to burn to a stub and be replaced, three times. Nothing came. A good watch is one the Remembrancer has nothing to write about.
Outsiders ask if it is dull. It is the opposite. It is a great many small careful things, and one very large thing that never comes. The waiting is the work.
The worst watch is the one after a quarrel. Two Ashwardens who have fallen out cannot call to each other, and the edge goes quiet in the wrong way. We make peace before the post. It is the rule.

lines.text: I watch. You are being watched. It is nothing personal, stranger. Everyone is watched. Some are watched more kindly.
I count the ghasts as they pass over the valley. They never come low. But I count them. It seems the least we can do for a grief that large.
My post is a basalt step worn smooth by the Ashwardens before me. I put my feet where theirs fit. It is like being greeted by every one of them in turn.
A Piglin scout came up the valley once, gold from helm to heel, bold as a lamp. I said the Vigil would remember he came. He left rather quickly.
I carry a small bone whistle I have never blown. If I blow it, the whole Vigil comes. Nobody wants to be the one who blew it for a stray Cairnback. I have heard of it happening.
On a long watch I say {kept}'s name once for every lantern I can see. It keeps the count steady. It also means I am never quite alone at my post. Not many guards can say that.
You may stand a watch with me, if you like. I will not ask you to guard anything. Only to stand where I can see you, which has become a pleasant place to look.
Would you like to know the only thing I fear on watch?

replies.text: Missing the one who comes in quietly because they mean no harm. A guard who watches too hard for enemies forgets to watch for friends.
I am a guard. Fear is the whole of the trade. I only wear it on the inside, like armour.
That is what outsiders say, just before something does. Please do not say it near the edge.

lines.text: May I ask why you wander the valley alone?

replies.text: Then you belong here. The quiet is the one thing we have in plenty, and we are glad to share it with someone who respects it.
Most people are. Look quietly, and do not step where the lanterns are lit for someone. That is all I ask.
Correct. I would still like to know. The edge must know who walks it, even if the edge is never told.

lines: A spear with a bone haft and a basalt head, taller than I am by an arm. Long enough to say stop, short enough to say it in a lane. A sword answers. A spear asks.
My breastplate is basalt, carved with the ribs of the Last Answer. It weighs as much as a small grief. I wear it so I never forget what I am standing in front of.
Every Ashwarden's circlet is shaped on their own brow by the Bonecarver, who measures with a length of cord and a very solemn face. Mine is a little loose. I am told that is my fault.
I carry a wide bone shield for standing in front of things. The first time I used it, it met a Piglin's thrown axe. The second, a stray Cairnback with a bad temper. The Cairnback hit harder.
A little ash on the palm gives a grip on a smooth haft. Ashwardens never wash their hands quite clean. It is called the warden's mark, and it is also laziness.
I wear soul-cloth wraps at wrist and shin. Slate, not black. Black shows against the ash. Slate looks like another piece of the valley, and a guard who is the valley cannot be told from it.
Everything we carry is plain. No gems, no ornament that catches the light. A Piglin will wear a hoard on their back and call it rank. We wear only what will not betray the post.
Our weapons have names, one to each, and the name goes on with the weapon when it passes to the next hand. Mine is called Hesper. Hesper has been in more quarrels than I have.

lines.text: What I carry is for the Vigil, not for you. You will not need to learn the difference, and I would take it as a kindness if you did not try.
May I show you how I hold the spear? There. The weight sits back, so the point can wait. A spear that wants to strike will strike. A spear that waits can be asked to stop.
I sharpen the head on a blackstone hone, slowly, saying names in time with the strokes. A blade sharpened to names stays sharp longer. I have no proof. I have no wish for any.
I borrowed a neighbour's spear for a drill once. It was all wrong in the hand. A spear learns its Ashwarden as a boot learns a foot. I gave it back politely and told no one.
Under the basalt I wear padded soul-cloth that a Brewer stitched for me, because the Brewer was bored. It is the most comfortable thing I own. I will hear no remarks on this.
My breastplate has a place inside, over the heart, where the carving is smooth. There I keep {kept}'s name, on a scrap, folded small. It has been in more fights than most Ashwardens.
If I am lost, my spear is to go to someone who will ask before they strike. I have thought on it. You ask before you strike. Do not tell my relatives I said so.
Would you care to hold it? Only the haft. The head is not for visitors.

replies.text: Good. Both hands. Lower the point. There. It is lighter than it looks, which is not a comfort.
Wise. Those who hold it learn what it weighs, and what it weighs on.
*does not move* No. Ask me again, as if you meant to be asked.

lines.text: People ask why we carry no bows. A bow looks for a target at a distance. A spear needs you to stand near. Which should a warden prefer?

replies.text: Yes. If I must hurt someone, I should have to look at them first. It is a very old rule and a wise one.
Whose safety? A bow keeps me safe. A spear keeps the question honest. I choose the honest one.

lines: Mostly the lost. Outsiders in bright armour, wandering into the valley with a map that is wrong and a plan that is worse. I turn them round gently. It saves everyone a funeral.
Piglin scouts, sometimes, in pairs, looking for the gold under the valley floor. They have been looking since the War. The valley has not changed its answer.
When a Hollowed stands at the rim, we stand also, and say nothing, and wait for it to turn. It always turns. I have never known whether to be relieved.
Magmari stand at the edge sometimes, dim from the walk, and ask for a fire. We give them a fire, and a long look to go with it. We do not give them our names. They do not ask for those.
A Weft came to the edge once, a long way off, and bowed to the Wall with all four arms. I did not know what to do. I bowed back with two. It seemed fair, and it seemed rude, and it was both.
Ghastkin drift past without a word, as they do, and I turn my face aside. They cry names away. I would rather they did not see mine.
The loudest visitors are the ones with a wither skull in the pack. They come in whispering. They always whisper. I have never learned why. I ask them to hand it over or turn back.
I ask three things of every stranger at the edge: who they are, what they carry, and whom they have lost. The third is the one they answer last, and truest.

lines.text: You are a visitor. I have decided that much. The rest is up to you. Walk slowly, and do not touch the lanterns.
I watched you cross the ash when you first came. You walked like someone afraid of the soul sand, which is sensible. I put you down as harmless. It is a note I have not had to change.
Two Piglin Brutes came up the lane once with a hewn log for a ram. We let them tire. Then the Remembrancer walked out and read them the Wall. They left. The log is still there. We use it as a bench.
I have been struck twice in all my watches, both times by someone I was not guarding against. A guard learns to watch the friendly face. The friendly face can be very quick.
Sometimes a Withren walks out past the edge and stands there, looking at nothing, for a long while. We let them. We stand a little closer. When they turn, we are already there.
The closest I came to failing was a child on the rim, hand out toward a wandering Hollowed. I got there in time. That child is an Ashwarden now. They never mention it. Neither do I.
If you come to the edge and I am not at my post, call my name, not the Vigil's. It is the one alarm I will not sleep through.
What would you do in my place, watching someone like you walk in?

replies.text: That is what I am doing. Kindly is a harder way to watch than it sounds. Thank you for noticing.
Trust is what the Wall is made of. It is earned one name at a time. Give me time.
*does not move* No. Ask again, politely, and the answer may change.

lines.text: I have never struck an outsider first. Do you think that wise, or weak?

replies.text: Weakness would have struck. Thank you. It is a lonely sort of rule, and it helps to have it agreed with.
I have been called so, by the living, who were not watching. I will keep the habit.

lines: I begin at the Hall, where the first lantern hangs, and go outward along each lane until the lights thin to nothing. Then I turn and do it back, to see what I missed. There is always something.
A round takes about as long as it takes to say the Wall once through, leaving out the long names. I do not leave out the long names. My rounds are slow.
I say each name aloud as I pass its lantern. Not loudly. The names are used to being said quietly. A shout, I think, would startle them.
A knotted cord hangs at my belt, one knot for each lantern, and it goes twice round my waist. When I lose count I run my fingers along it, and the knots remember for me.
The lanterns on the outer lanes burn lowest, because nobody walks there. I give them the most care. A name no one passes is a name in danger.
The oldest lantern in the Vigil hangs by the Hall. Nobody remembers who lit it first. I tend it first on every round, and say its name last. It is a small joke between me and it.
Near the terraces I check each chain twice. The Cairnbacks lean on the posts. I do not blame the Cairnbacks. I blame the posts, for being so leanable.
I never walk the same side of a lane twice running. The lanterns on the left have different stories from those on the right, and I would not like either side to feel overlooked.

lines.text: Keep to the middle of the lane, please, and touch nothing that hangs. Every lantern belongs to someone, and they cannot tell you off themselves.
I like the round past the wart terraces, where the lanterns throw their blue on the plants. The wart looks as though it is being told a secret. I think it likes the names.
I reached the end of a round once and found I had said one name twice and missed another. I walked all the way back to find the missed one. I said it three times, to be fair.
A few lanterns burn for names that are waiting for a child to choose them. They hang closest to the Hall. I trim those first, because they are the ones who are waiting.
When I walk the lanes in the quiet, I listen. A lantern with a name it likes burns steady. I cannot prove it. A neighbour calls it nonsense. A neighbour's lanterns flicker.
{kept}'s lantern is on the third lane, by the bone post with the notch. I stop there longest. I do not know if they hear. I have decided it is rude to doubt.
I have a lantern ready for you, unlit, on a hook by my door. It will be lit when you are gone. I am in no hurry to light it. Please make me wait.
Would you walk a round with me? It is slow, and you must be silent, and you will learn nothing but names.

replies.text: Come, then. Walk where I walk. If a lantern gutters, stop, and say the name I give you. Say it as if they were standing just behind you.
Everything is, for those who rush. Come back when you are ready to be slow. The lanterns will not have gone anywhere.

lines.text: Which would you rather be, the lantern or the one who keeps it?

replies.text: A fair choice. The lantern is remembered by everyone who passes. The keeper is remembered by the lantern, which is a smaller audience.
Then you understand the job. A lantern is lit for one. The keeper is lit by all of them. It is lonelier and warmer than it sounds.

lines: A long pole with a bone hook on the end, for lifting a lantern down without climbing. I made three before I made one that did not bend. The other two are fence posts now.
Wick-shears, small and sharp and mine. I have trimmed a thousand wicks with them. Lend them to a neighbour and they come back dull. I do not lend them.
A snuffer cup on a short handle, for the Relighting and no other day. I put each light out myself and say its name loudly as I do, so it knows it will be lit again. I do not enjoy it.
A rag of soul-cloth in my sleeve, for wiping the glass. Lanterns gather ash. Ash on the glass dims the light. I like to think it dims the name. It does not, but I wipe it anyway.
The chains are iron, got by a long trade I will not describe. I check each link on my round. A lantern that falls is a name that falls, and nobody wants to stand near that.
A covered lamp of fire taken from a Cairnback's bowl. When a lantern goes out I light it from that, never from flint. A name should be lit from a living fire, not struck out of stone.
A stub of candle in my belt, for finding my way home if the lanterns on my own lane were dark. It has only ever been used when they were not. I carry it for comfort.
My ladder is bone and old, and creaks a name of its own. I call it Sigh. I was wrong about its weight once. The Bonecarver replaced three rungs, and has forgiven me.

lines.text: Tools are for the work. Please do not pick them up. A hook in the wrong hand is a bent hook.
Lanterns for names that a child has chosen hang a little lower, at a child's eye. When they look up at the light and say the name the first time, I stand behind them, pretending to trim something.
I tried to make my own wicks once, from wart-fibre. They burned bright and fast, and every lantern on the lane sneezed. I buy my wicks now. Some crafts are best left to others.
I know each lantern by the note it gives when I tap its frame. Together they would make a tune. I have never written it down. I think the tune is the Wall, played all at once.
The Bonecarver makes my hooks, and I pay them in news of the lanes. It is an old trade. We never speak of the price. It would spoil it.
The pole I carry was my master's. The hook is worn bright where their hand held it. I put mine in the same place. We are the same height, which seemed a sign.
I would give you my second pair of shears, if you wanted them. You would trim a wick well. I would trust you with a light, and I trust very few with a light.
Would you like to try the hook? It is lighter than it looks. The trick is lifting without looking up.

replies.text: Hold it low and lift slowly. Do not rush the chain. There. You have lifted a name and set it down again. That is the whole of the art.
Everyone fears that. I have dropped it, on the Remembrancer's foot. It was forgiven. Try.

lines.text: Which is the best tool a keeper owns?

replies.text: A good guess, and wrong. It is only a stick that learned a trick.
Closer. Sharp things get the credit. But no.
Yes. And the worst tool to own, because it cannot be bought, sharpened or lent. Well answered.

topics.ask: What if a light goes out?
lines: First I check the wick. Then the glass. Then the chain. Then, if all three are sound, I check the name. A light does not go out for no reason. It goes out for a dull one, or a sad one.
Most outages are wicks. The rest are Cairnbacks, children or outsiders. A small number are none of these, and those I take to the Remembrancer, with my hood in my hands.
I say the name until it catches. Sometimes the first time. Sometimes the fortieth. I have found no way to hurry it. I have found several ways to try.
A dark lantern in a lit lane is the loudest thing in the Vigil. Passers-by lower their voices without knowing why. Then they remember, and look up, and say the name. That is what lanterns are for.
The worst in my time was seven at once, from a draught down the lane. I walked it saying seven names while my hands shook. It cost me all the breath I had.
I once relit the wrong lantern. Right name, wrong hook. The Remembrancer noticed within a breath and said nothing, which was far worse than the shouting I had prepared for.
A lantern that will not catch needs asking. I go and find the keeper and ask whether the name is still being said. It always is, or almost. The almost is the reason I make the walk.
Children are the worst for putting lights out. They blow on them, to see what happens. What happens is that I run. I do not blame them. It is a fine lantern for blowing on.

lines.text: If a lantern goes out near you, say nothing and fetch me. Do not try to light it. A lit name is a promise, and a stranger's promise is not what the name asked for.
If you see one go dark and I am far off, hold your hand near it and say any name you carry. It will not catch. But it will know someone stood by. That is half the work.
When the Hall is full of voices saying the Wall, the air presses, and a few lanterns gutter. I take it as a compliment. The names got up to listen.
When I was new, I panicked at every flicker. My master said a flicker is only a lantern clearing its throat. I have lived by that for a long while, and been wrong only twice.
A dark lantern is not a lost name. I tell myself so on every round. The name is on the Wall, in the Remembrancer, in the keeper and in me. Four places. A lantern is only a fifth.
Once {kept}'s lantern went out. I stood under it a long while, and when it caught, my face was damp. It was soul-mist off the sand. Yes. Soul-mist.
The lantern I keep ready for you does not flicker, being unlit. If it ever does, I will drop everything and run to find you. I have practised the running.
Shall I teach you the words I say? There are only a few. It is the saying that does the work.

replies.text: Say the name as though the person were just behind you. Say it with a little warmth, as to a friend. That is all. Most keepers overcomplicate it.
No. A name said by proxy is a name half said. But I will stand beside you. That I can do.

lines.text: Does a dark lantern frighten you, as it does me?

replies.text: Good. A Withren who says otherwise has not been looking.
Only fire. As the Wither was only fire. Mind your words near lanterns.

lines: You press the seed into the soul sand with your thumb, to the first knuckle. Not the second. The second is too deep, and the wart sulks. The first is exactly right.
Wart has four stages: a nub, a leaf, a knot and a crown. The crown is the only one worth harvesting. The other three are worth watching, which is the actual work.
You cannot hurry it. Light and shouting do nothing. Wart ripens at its own pace, and that pace is the pace of the dead: slow, steady and totally indifferent to how much you want it.
I sing to it, a little. Names, mostly. I say the Wall in rows, one row to each terrace. The wart has never yet been late. I do not claim the two are related.
Bone meal does nothing for wart. I tried it for a whole growing. The wart looked at me and carried on at its own speed. Some things do not take advice.
I never harvest the whole row. I leave the crowns at each end to seed the next, and I thank them. The ends of a row are its elders. They are slow and stubborn and bear the best.
The soul sand must be turned with a bone fork, never an iron one. The old growers say iron makes it forget. I do not know. I have never wished to find out.
The best crown from each terrace I carry to the Brewer myself. The rest go in the baskets. The smallest I eat on the spot, raw. It tastes of something sharp that was once green.

lines.text: Wart needs soul sand, patience and no visitors. I mean that kindly. Please stand on the path, and keep your boots out of my rows.
Come and see the knots on the edge of the third terrace. Not touching. Just looking. In the right light wart looks like a handful of small, careful lanterns. I do my best work unwatched.
I plant by the sound of the soul sand. A bed that whispers is ready. A bed that is silent wants more time. The whole valley whispers, and it took me a long while to hear which whisper was the soil's.
I planted a row in the wrong order once, and it came up in a crooked line that looked, to me, like a name. I did not say whose. I told the Remembrancer. We agreed I was tired.
A good grower has dirty hands and a clean mind. I have the first. The second I am working on. The terraces are good teachers because they never praise you.
Every terrace has one row tended for a name. Mine is for {kept}. The wart in that row is the best on the terrace. I give no credit to the wart. I give all of it to {kept}.
If you ever want wart, take it from the row at the end of the third terrace. I have told the others it is my share. It will always be yours. Do not tell them either.
Would you like to plant one? Thumb, first knuckle, no further. Then you may name it.

replies.text: There. Now it is yours, and mine, and the soil's. Do not give it a dreadful name. It will live a long while.
Watching is half of growing. The other half is not stepping on things. You are well on your way.

lines.text: Do you know why the old growers sing to wart?

replies.text: The answer for visitors. It is wrong, but it is gentle, and visitors are rarely ready for the right one.
Yes. The wart does not listen. The soul sand might. It costs us only breath, and we have breath.

lines: Each terrace is a step cut into the valley wall and held up by a retaining wall of stacked basalt. A good wall needs no mortar. It needs only to be built by someone who is afraid of what lies below.
We name the terraces for the dead who first worked the slope: the Long Step, the Stooped Terrace, Varen's Reach. The names are older than the wart, and may be older than the walls.
Soul sand slows whoever walks on it, so the paths are laid basalt, a stone wide. Stepping off the path is allowed once. After that the terrace speaks to you, and the grower speaks more loudly.
Every terrace has a drain cut along its foot, because soul sand holds on to everything, mist most of all, and wart hates a damp foot. I dig them out each Vigil. It is not a glamorous office.
The Cairnbacks graze the terraces in turn, never two on the same step. They always take the best crown first. Having opinions about wart is what makes them Cairnbacks. I plant two for them.
The oldest terrace is the Long Step, and it sags. We hold it up with a great many stones and a certain amount of hope. The hope, I am told, is the stronger of the two.
Terrace work is back work. I am bent for good, and I have decided not to mind. There is dignity in a stoop. The tall ones all look over the wart. I look at it.
At harvest the whole Vigil comes to the terraces. Baskets pass hand to hand down the steps, nobody speaks, and every basket is counted twice. Oddly like a funeral, and a good deal merrier.

lines.text: Please stay on the laid stone. It is a path, it is wide enough, and it has been walked in good order for longer than anyone has kept count.

I will show you the Empty Step, the terrace we have never planted. We keep it bare so that something in the valley is always waiting. Do not ask me what for. I do not know. I only know it should wait.
From the top terrace the wart makes a pattern like ribs. We did not plan it. We plant by the lie of the land. The land, it seems, remembers the Last Answer too.
In my first Vigils I built a step wrong, and the whole terrace slid in the first ashfall. I spent every breath I had for a long Vigil moving stones. I now build as if the wall were listening.
At the top of the highest terrace stands a bone post with a notch for every harvest. It belongs to no one. Whoever brings in the last crown of a harvest cuts a notch. I have cut eleven.
I come out to the terraces when a name is heavy in me. The wart asks nothing. It is the best company I know, apart from the present one.
I have never taken anyone to the terrace behind the third wall. The wart there grows crooked and sweet. If you come, bring nothing. It does not like visitors with plans.
Would you carry a basket down? It is easier than it looks. It is also harder than it looks. Both are true of most honest work.

replies.text: Good. Keep it level. Do not look at the drop. Count your steps, and say a name for each. The name makes the basket lighter. Not the wart. The name.
Then you have already joined the Stooped Terrace, in spirit. Sit on the wall and tell me how it is done.

lines.text: Do you suppose the wart knows it is for the brewery?

replies.text: Nor I. I try not to mention it. It would take it hard.
Probably not. That is the mercy of plants. They do not ask where the road goes.

lines: Hoglins, if a Piglin herd strays over the ridge. They root up a whole step in one visit. I do not blame the hoglins. I blame whoever lets a hoglin wander.
Ghast fire. A ghast crying over a terrace can burn a step in a breath. We bank what is left and stand silent. We do not curse it. It is our grief, and it has every right to be loud.
The curl. A leaf comes up grey and curled in on itself, and then so does the next. It spreads along a row like a rumour. I tear it out at once. Then I sit by the hole and say sorry.
Soul sand gets tired. Plant it too long and it sulks, and the crowns come up thin. So I rest a bed for as long as it takes to say its row of the Wall three times. Then it forgives me.
Boots. I have said it a hundred times. A terrace is not a road. Yet every so often an outsider comes through with a pack and a plan and a pair of boots, and a row is gone.
Ash settles on the upper terraces and lies on the leaves. I wipe each leaf by hand. It takes a very long time. I find it restful, so long as nobody speaks to me.
Gossip in the rows. Two growers talk, and the work slows. A slow row is a late row. Then the crop is short, and the Brewer comes to find out why, and finds us still talking.
Idleness, in the grown. They look at a row, say it is fine, and leave. A row is never fine. A row is a thing that has not yet failed.

lines.text: My crop has troubles, and you are not one of them yet. Let us keep it that way, with your feet on the path.
The worst enemy is impatience, and it is mine. I check the knots every few breaths, which does nothing. The wart goes on. Then the crowns come exactly when they meant to.
The whole third terrace went grey in a single stretch once. I thought it was the curl. It was an outsider's spilled potion. They apologised for a very long time. We let them.
Cairnbacks lean on the retaining walls to scratch their shells, and over many Vigils it bows a wall. I set scratching posts at the end of each row. They ignore the posts. They prefer a challenge.
A blight is a kind of grief. You look at the row and see where the wart is not, and you say the name of each missing crown. Do not laugh. It works. The next planting comes in strong.
I lost a whole terrace to ghast fire once. I stood in the black stubble and said nothing. {kept} would have known what to say. I said their name instead. It turned out to be the right thing.
If a terrace ever fails so badly that I cannot go on, I would like you to be there. Not to help. Only to be someone else who saw it. A blight is lighter when two are looking.
What would you do if the whole crop failed?

replies.text: Yes. That is the whole art, in two words. I should cut it into a post.
Briefly. Then plant. The wart does not mourn. It simply starts again, which is the better example.
Then the Brewer would go without, and the Hall would go unfed, and you would be sorry. You may be sorry. You may not be a grower.

lines.text: Have you heard the story of the terrace that grew only one crown?

replies.text: The grower would plant no more. One crown, one name, was enough, they said. The terrace stayed bare. We still visit it. Nobody knows whether they were wise.
Very well. It is a short story with a long ending. It will keep.

lines: A basalt rasp for the first shape, a bone awl for the details, and a blackstone hone for everything the awl has done badly. The hone is the tool I trust most. It forgives.
The bow-drill makes the small holes: toggles, lantern eyes, the loops on a stole. A cord, a bone shaft and a twist of the wrist. It is the only tool I own that sings.

My mallet is a single knuckle of old valley bone, polished by hands until it is the colour of candle wax. It was my master's, and their master's. It fits no hand but mine now, which I find rude of it.
I wear a veil of soul-cloth when I rasp. Bone dust is as fine as ash and as patient as grief. It gets in everywhere and stays. I breathed a good deal of it before I learned.
A bone saw is only a flat rib with teeth cut in it. I cut the teeth myself, in a slow stretch with nothing else to do. It saws very well, and complains the whole time.
My dividers are two thin bone legs on a pin, for stepping out measures. A Vigil is built to a Withren's stride: lane posts a stride apart, plinths three. They know our stride better than we do.
A hooked scraper, for the insides of things: skull-bowls, lantern cups. It is the quietest of my tools. It leaves a surface like a held breath.
Every tool has a hole in its handle for hanging, and I hang them in the same order. When one is missing, the gap is the first thing I see. A gap in a row is a loss. I take that personally.

lines.text: Do not touch the tools, please. They are sharp, and they are mine, and some of them are older than I am.
I will let you hold the awl. Careful. It is a fine thing, and a mean one if the wrist is wrong. Hold it as you would a feather you did not wish to bend. There. You hold it well. Tell no one.
I lost the awl once and searched the whole workshop. It was in my hand. I do not discuss this. Please do not discuss this.
I keep one chisel for the plinths in the Hall, and it touches nothing else. It has been honed so many times it is a third of its first size. Every sharpening was a name said.
When a tool breaks in the middle of a cut, I stop and say nothing for a while. Then I begin again with a different tool. I have learned that a broken tool is not an accident. It is advice.
The awl I carry belonged to the keeper of {kept} before me. It came with the name. I use it every time I carve. It is a very good awl, and I think it likes the work.
When I am gone my tools go on the workshop wall in their usual order, with a gap for each I wore out. You will always be welcome to take one down. That is what a gap means.
Shall I show you how a rasp bites? Bone is kinder than it looks, but it holds a grudge.

replies.text: Long strokes, even pressure. Let the tool do the speaking. Good. You have the first patience, which is the hard one.
That is fine. Watching is how I learned. You will learn more from my mistakes than from your own.

lines.text: Which of my tools do you think is the oldest?

replies.text: Yes. It was old when my master got it. It has outlived them all, it will outlive me, and it still has every bit of its bone.
A good guess. A stone is older than everything. But that hone is the newest thing in the workshop. I traded for it.

lines: From the valley floor. Old ribs and long spines lie half buried in the soul sand, the bones of beasts so ancient nobody kept them. I walk the valley after the ground shifts and see what is uncovered.
There is a rule: we ask before we dig. Not the bone. The ground. I kneel and say that I mean no harm, and I wait. It is a small courtesy. The valley has been very good to me.
Fresh bone is no use. It must lie a long time. I choose bone the ash has weathered until it rings like a bell when tapped. Anything that does not ring is not ready, or is not bone.
I never take the whole of a thing. Of every great rib I leave the first and last hand's-breadth in the ground. They are the part the beast would want to keep. I cannot prove this, either.
The great Ribs along the valley wall are the best. They arch a full height above a Withren, and nobody knows what they belonged to. I have asked the Remembrancer. The Remembrancer has asked the Ribs.
Never a person's bone. Never. If I find one that is not a beast's, I put down everything and go to the Remembrancer. It happens more than I would like, in the valleys near the fortresses.
I tell beast from person by the weight. A person's bone is lighter and sings a higher note. I learned it from my master, who had it from theirs. Nobody has needed to check it since.
Some bone is brought by travellers from valleys I will never see. I check it three times, and then once more for manners.

lines.text: Bone comes from the valley and goes to the Vigil. That is all I will say to a stranger. Bone is not a thing to idle over.
I will show you the Bone Walk, if you like: a long loop of the valley where the best bone lies. We say nothing the whole way, and I come back lighter than I left.
I found a rib once bigger than any that has fallen from the Ribs, and carried it two lanes before I saw I had no use for it. I set it upright by the road. It is a bench-post now. Children climb it.
The best bone I ever found was a single vertebra, round as a bowl, with a hollow on top that held a little dust. I made it the lantern cup at the head of the third lane.
I have a friend in the valley whom I have never seen. I leave a toggle on a rock, and when I return it is gone, and a clean rib lies in its place. I do not ask. It is a good arrangement.
I take {kept} with me on the Bone Walk, in my head, and tell them what I am looking for. They like the long ones best, I think. I always bring one of the long ones home for them.
If you ever find a bone you cannot name, bring it to me. Not to sell. To ask. There is always a story under it, and you are good at hearing stories.
People ask if it is lonely work, walking the valley with a sack. Is it?

replies.text: It is. It is also grim. The valley is a place where the two are old friends, and I am a guest at their table.
It is grim, and peaceful as well. You have heard both halves. Most visitors only hear one.

lines.text: Would I carve a bone that an outsider brought me? That depends on what it is.

replies.text: Bring it. If it is a beast's, I will carve it and say your name over the first cut. It is a small honour. I give it rarely.
Show me. If it was a person's, we will take it quietly to the Remembrancer. If a beast's, we will thank it and carve it. Thank you for bringing it, and not selling it.

lines: Toggles for a new run of soul-cloth coats. A small thing, made a hundred times. The hundredth is as careful as the first, or it is not a toggle, it is a lie.
A post for the fourth lane. It leans, being bone, and I let it lean a little. A post that stands too straight looks as if it is not listening.
I rough out the shape and then let the bone rest. It must settle a good while before the finish, or it warps. You cannot hurry a bone any more than a grief.
I finish with soul-cloth, rubbed in small circles, until the surface is smooth enough to hold a face. It takes a very long time. Nobody has ever thanked me for the underside.
I never sign a piece. A carver's mark on a thing made for the dead is like a shout in the Hall. Where my thumb pressed hardest the grain shows, and that is signature enough.
The frame for a new sign on the Wall is the last thing a carver gives a Withren: a plain bone border, no more. The sign is the Remembrancer's. The frame is mine. I cut each one slowly.
A Weft once asked to see my work. I showed them a bone needle I had made as an exercise. They turned it over and over and said it was a good needle. I took it back and broke it. It was a good needle.
My master carved one toggle, plain, the same each time. Every Withren in the Vigil wears one. They made it a little better each time, and nobody could say how.

lines.text: I am carving. Do not stand in my light, please. The bone does not know you yet.
I like to carve what is not seen: the underside of a plinth, the back of a post. The dead notice, I think. The living never look. Both are fine audiences.
The children want skulls, always. I make them small, with no teeth and a hole in the back for string. It is the hardest work I do. A child knows at once if you are not trying.
I cracked a plinth once by hurrying. A hairline, no more. I told the Remembrancer, and we filled it with soot from the Hall's own fire. The crack is now the most looked-at part of the plinth.
A bad cut is not a mistake. It is the bone telling you where it wished to be left alone. I have learned to listen. I have also learned to keep a second piece of bone.
I carved a small bone bird for {kept} once, and set it under their sign on the Wall. It is still there. Nobody has taken it away, and nobody has asked. A fine arrangement.
I have one piece unfinished that I will not show you: a small toggle with the first stroke of your name cut into the back. It is not for the Wall. It is for when you are not in a hurry.
Would you like to see what I am making? It is not finished, and I am not finished with it.

replies.text: Here. Do not breathe on it. It is a bird, or it will be. The bone has already decided about the wings. I am only catching up.
Another time, then. It will not mind. Bone is the most patient material there is, and I am working on the rest of me.

lines.text: What do you think a carved thing is for, if the dead cannot use it?

replies.text: Partly. The living need something to hold while they remember. A toggle is a small hand to hold.
Also true. They gave us the bone, in a way. It would be rude to forget that.
You are not entirely wrong. It is for nothing, which is why it matters. Useful things are used up. Useless things stay.

lines: Three kinds, mostly. The Mending, for the living who are hurt. The Fireward, for crossing fire. And the warm one, for those who come into the brewery with nowhere else to take it.
The warm one, properly Steadying, is only wart and a pinch of fire, steeped slowly. It does nothing. That is its virtue. You hold it, and it is warm, and nobody asks you anything.
The Mending wants patience and a steady hand. A brew wrong by a pinch heals the wrong thing. I once healed a bruise and it came straight back, out of spite.
The Fireward I brew rarely, and always with a witness. It lets the drinker walk through fire. The witness is there to remember who walked in, in case someone does not walk out.
I will not brew with gold. It is the Piglins' metal, and we are agreed on that. So no sharp sight in the dark for us. We have lanterns.
I will not use a ghast tear either, though the Mending would run sweeter with one. A tear is a grief somebody else has let go. In a Vigil that is a poor ingredient.
Every brew begins with a base, clear and still, and we do not discuss where it comes from. It is clean. It asks nothing. It is the only thing in the brewery I would rather not look at.
Brewing is mostly waiting and listening. A good brew sings one low note when it is ready. I have trained my ear to it. A brew that sings two notes is a different story.

lines.text: I brew for the Vigil first. If you are hurt, ask the Remembrancer, who will ask me. It is slow, but that is how a brew gets decided.
If you are ever badly hurt near here, send word. I keep a Mending stoppered by the door for exactly that. It is for the living who knock, and I am glad it is used rarely.
I invented a drink once called Quiet. It made everyone in the brewery silent for a stretch. They loved it. The Remembrancer banned it, on the grounds that silence should not be bottled.
The best brew I ever made was an accident: a cracked bottle, a leaning flame, a smell like warm bone. It healed nothing. Everyone who smelled it sat down and told me about someone.
I measure by the joint of my thumb: one of wart, two of fire. It suits no other thumb. My apprentice measures by theirs. We make the same brew from different thumbs.
I keep a bottle of the first Mending I ever made, set by for {kept}. I know they cannot drink it. I look at it when the work is heavy.
For you I would break my rule on tears. If you were bleeding and nothing else worked, I would go to the Ghastkin myself, with my head bowed. Do not make me. I would do it.
Would you taste the warm one? It is harmless. It is also, in my experience, the best thing I make.

replies.text: There. It does nothing. Holding the cup is the point. You see? Now stay as long as you like. The bench is yours.
It is only wart and a pinch of fire. It is as safe as a bone. Which is to say, mostly.

lines.text: If you could only make one, which would you choose: the Mending, the Fireward, or the warm one?

replies.text: Practical. The living are always hurt. You would make a fine Brewer, and a dull companion at a Vigil.
A bold choice. Fire is a thing the living keep walking into. I dislike it, but I admire the nerve.
The right answer, and the one nobody gives. The Mending heals a wound. The warm one heals the waiting.

lines: A brewing stand of bone and basalt, with a blaze rod at its heart. It holds three bottles at a time. Three is the Three's number, and I try not to read too much into that.
Glass bottles in rows, each stoppered with a plug of wart-fibre. I count them whenever I begin. The count is how I know a bottle has walked off. Bottles do walk, at a Vigil.
A bone ladle, a bone spoon and a bone stirrer, for different things and all one colour. Brewers mix them up in the end. The spoon has been in the Mending. The ladle has not forgiven me.
A basalt pestle and mortar for crushing wart. The mortar has a hollow worn smooth by many hands. I think of them while I grind. It helps the grinding and does nothing for the brew.
A slate with chalk marks: how much, how long, how it went. Every batch is written down. A brew that went well and was not written down is the saddest kind.
Blaze powder in a stoppered jar. I keep it well away from the soul lantern, and the soul lantern well away from me. We maintain a respectful triangle.
One stool, no more. A second stool means a second person, and a second person means talking, and talking means a spill.
A shelf at the back under a sheet. Nothing on it is ready, and nothing on it may be touched. A few bottles have been there longer than I have. They are making up their minds.

lines.text: That is my bench, and those are my bottles. Look as you like. Touch nothing, taste nothing, and please do not ask what is under the sheet.
You may sit on the stool, once. It has held only three people besides me. All three were grieving, and I did not mind. Now it is yours for a moment.
I mark my stoppers with notches, not words. One notch is the Mending. Two is the Fireward. A smooth stopper is the warm one. A cracked stopper is a bottle I do not trust.
My best bottle is a plain one with a thumb-sized dent. It was my master's. They dropped it once and it did not break, and they said that was how it chose them. I use it for the first pour.
The blaze rod in my stand was a gift from an Ashwarden, taken from a fortress where it had no use. I think about that rod often. I wonder what it was guarding.
Under the bench I keep a small box of burnt pots, one from every failed batch, in order. A bench with no failures on it has never been used. I also keep them to stay humble.
There is a bottle under the sheet with your name on the stopper. I will not say what is in it. I will say it is the one thing I made on purpose for someone who was not hurt.
Would you hold a bottle? Gently. They are warm.

replies.text: There. Feel that? That is a brew thinking. You are holding a thought somebody has not finished. Hand it back before it decides anything.
Then do not. I have enough broken glass for three Vigils. Come close and look, and be at peace.

lines.text: People say a brewery ought to be cold and clean. Mine is warm and cluttered. Which would you trust?

replies.text: Then you would trust a bone with nobody in it. The clutter is where the living are.
Good. A cold brewery is a cellar. A warm one is a kitchen for the heart.

lines: Often. Everyone does. A brewer who has never made something awful has never made anything. The trick is to make it in small quantities.
My first batch as a learner was all wart and no fire. It sat in the bottle and did nothing, loudly. My master said it was the most honest brew they had ever tasted.
I once mixed up two stoppers and handed a mourner the Fireward. They walked straight into a soul fire to see if it worked. It worked. They have forgiven me, and were not hurt.
A bad brew smells of regret. A good brew smells of nothing at all. Brewers prize the nothing. I have spent a lifetime chasing it, and I have caught it twice.
A batch went sour once and stood in a corner for a whole Vigil. The smell crept out, and the Remembrancer came to ask who had died. I said nobody, yet. We kept the door shut.
The Tearkeepers of the Ghastkin brew healing too, with a single grief. It is quicker than mine, and they will tell you so. Mine does not take the memory with it. We do not discuss which is better.
A Magmari traded me a lump of magma cream once for the Fireward. I said the recipe was not mine to give, and kept the cream. I regret nothing, and the cream was excellent.
The worst mistake is not a bad batch. It is a good batch given to the wrong person. A Mending can mend the wrong thing. I now ask twice who is hurt, and where.

lines.text: That is not a story for strangers. Mistakes are shared with those who have earned them. I will say only that the floor was never the same.
I forgot a brew once, and it stood so long that it began to sing. I put it on the shelf and covered it. It is singing still. I am afraid to find out what about.
My master once added a pinch of ash to a Mending, as a joke. It cured every ill in the brewery and gave everyone a cough. We have not repeated it. We have not forgotten it either.
I nearly lost the brewery to a flame once. A bottle cracked, the blaze powder caught, and I stood there and said the Wall. Not my best idea. The flame went out of its own accord, from boredom.
The mistake I am proudest of is the Fireward. It was meant to be a Mending, and it came out too hot, and it was a different brew entirely. All the best brews are mistakes that were paid attention to.
The mistake I regret was a Mending I finished too slowly. The one who needed it was gone before it sang. I keep the bottle still. I have not found the way to empty it.
If I ever make a mistake with your life, I will not forgive myself. You need not forgive me either. We will both be difficult about it. That is what friends are for.
Shall I tell you the very worst brew I know? It has a quiet name.

replies.text: Keening. Wart without the fire, only the mood. It does nothing but make you sad in the gentlest way. We banned it. It is still in great demand.
Wise. Some recipes are best left in the pot.

lines.text: Do you make mistakes?

replies.text: Good. You and I will get on. It is the ones who say never that I check on.
Then you are lying, or you are doing nothing. Neither is a good sign at my bench.

topics.ask: What will you be when grown?
lines: Everyone asks that! I do not know yet. I have to try them all first. I tried the Remembrancer's hood. It smelled of old ash.
I want to be an Ashwarden! You get a spear and a circlet and you get to say stop. I practise saying stop. Nobody has stopped yet.
I want to be a Lantern-keeper. You get to say a name to every lantern, and nobody tells you off for talking. I would talk all through a round.
Wart-grower, maybe. You get dirt. All the dirt you want. You also get a bad back, they say, but I am small, so I have time.
Bonecarver! They make skulls, and the little ones are for children. I would make the best skull and be told it was too good. It happens.
A Brewer, because the brewery is the warmest room. If I am a Brewer I live there. I would sleep next to the pots. I would be very warm and very smelly.
Remembrancer, but that is for old ones. I will have to be old first. I am working on it. It is the slowest job in the world.
I do not want to be a Hollowed. I told {neighbour} that, and they said nobody wants to. I said I was only checking.

lines.text: That is a secret. I do not know you well enough yet. Ask me again and I will pick something, just to be polite.
Do you have a job? Outsiders must. What is it? Is it better than mine? Mine is only being a child. It is a very small job, but I am very good at it.
I told the Remembrancer I want to be a Remembrancer. They said first I must remember where I left my boots. I did not know where they were. I have not been told again.
I changed my mind four times along one lane. I started as an Ashwarden and ended as a Brewer. The Brewer is the only one who gave me anything to hold.
I think I will be a Wart-grower, because wart does not mind how tall you are. It does not look up at you. It is the only thing here that does not.
I want to be good at one thing. One thing, all the way down. Grown-ups say one thing is enough. I think they say it because they only have the one.
When I am grown and have a post, I will let you visit me there. Even if it is the Wall. Even if it is dull. You can sit down, and I will tell you everything.
Which job would you pick for me?

replies.text: Oh! That is one of mine. You listen well. I will say the first name for you, when I have the pole.
I knew you would say that. I look like I could. Stand back. I am practising stop.
Warm and smelly. You know me too well.

lines.text: Is it hard, choosing? It feels like I will be it for ever.

replies.text: Can I? The grown-ups say never. I will ask them again, politely, with my hands behind my back.
I will. I will choose so well that they put it on the Wall under my name. Later. Much later.

lines: I carry baskets at harvest. Small ones. The wart does not know the difference. I think it is easier to be small. You get to carry the little things.
I sweep the bone dust off the workshop floor. It comes right back. The Bonecarver says that is the whole point of floors.
I hold the lantern pole steady when the Lantern-keeper climbs. I am very good at holding. I have not let go once. Well, once. We do not talk about it.
At the brewery I stir. Only stir. Not taste. They watch my mouth the whole time. I think it is the most trusted job in the Vigil.
I fetch the Remembrancer's brush. They set it down on the Wall's step, and then they look for it. I find it every time. It is always where they were just standing.
I rub the soot off the lantern glass at my end of the lane, with my sleeve. The Lantern-keeper says use the rag. The rag is always elsewhere. My sleeve is always there.
I polish the Ashwarden's boots, in turn, because a clean boot is a sharp boot. I do not see how. But the Ashwarden has never let me touch the spear.
I carry messages between the terraces and the brewery. The wart is ready is the best one. The wart is late is the one where I run.

lines.text: I am not allowed to say what my chores are to strangers. It might be a secret. Or it might be that I have not done them yet.
I get to light the little lamps by the door of the Hall. Not the Three's. Not those. But I say the Three's names anyway, very small, in case they are listening.
Sometimes it is the same chore twice, because the first time I did it badly. Grown-ups call that practice. It is the same as doing it twice.
I am better at chores than I let on. I leave a few things undone so the grown-ups feel needed. Do not tell them. It is a kindness.
The best chore is carrying a message to someone. Orwen is lit. Brannoch is mended. It feels like carrying something very important and quite heavy and made of nothing.
The Brewer gave me a whole bottle and said I must not open it until I am grown. I shake it sometimes. It sounds like a secret. I am keeping it safe, which is a chore of its own.
If you ever want help with a chore, I will do it. Even the dull ones. Even the bone dust. I would sweep a whole workshop for you, and not complain for as long as it took to complain.
Would you do my chores? Only the sweeping.

replies.text: Really? You are the best outsider I know. Of two. Do not sweep the plinths. They are not mine to sweep.
That is what the Bonecarver says. I am beginning to suspect they are right.

lines.text: Do you do chores where you come from?

replies.text: Then you are nearly one of us. We have not had one before.
None? What do you do all the time? Is it terribly dull? Or terribly nice?

lines: The Ashwarden, from behind the third post. They stand so still. I tried it. I lasted as long as it takes to say one name. They lasted the whole watch.
The Lantern-keeper, because their hands know where every chain is without looking. I closed my eyes once and tried. I walked into a Cairnback.
The Bonecarver, because the dust floats in the light like little ghosts. I know they are not ghosts. But I ask each one to be quiet, just in case.
The Remembrancer, from under the table. They do not know I am there. Their lips move when they remember, as if they were tasting the names.
The Brewer, from the door. If I stand in the door, the Brewer pretends not to see me, and hands me a cup. It is the best arrangement in the Vigil.
The Wart-grower, because they talk to the wart. Their voice goes quiet and kind. It is the same voice they use at the Wall. I want a voice like that.
I watch who shoos me. The Bonecarver shoos hardest, then the Brewer, then the Ashwarden, who does not shoo, only turns. That is the worst. I would rather be shooed.
Everyone has a face they make when they work. The Ashwarden's is empty. The Lantern-keeper's is soft. The Bonecarver's frowns. The Brewer's is secretly a smile. I have not told the Brewer.

lines.text: I do not watch strangers. I watch grown-ups who do the same thing every time. You are not that. Yet.
I watch you too, a bit. You look at the lanterns like you want to ask about them. You can. I know most of them.
My favourite thing to watch is someone doing what they love when they think nobody is looking. The Brewer humming. The Bonecarver stroking a rib. The Ashwarden smiling at a Cairnback.
I learned to light a lantern by watching. I did not touch it. I watched until I could do it in my head. Then I did it for real, in the wrong place, and the Lantern-keeper laughed.
The Remembrancer caught me watching once. They said: good. Watching is the first half of remembering. The second half is doing it again. I have been doing the second half ever since.
If I could be any grown-up for a short while, I would be the one who knows when to be quiet. I have not found out who that is. I think it may be all of them.
I watch the lane for you now. When I see you coming, I run to tell the others. It is my own job. I made it myself. I am very good at it.
Do you want to watch with me? You must hide, and be very still.

replies.text: Good! Behind the post. No, further. Closer. Shh. Watch the Brewer's hands. See? It is like a dance, but with bottles.
You are! Crouch lower. Pretend you are a terrace.

lines.text: Have you ever been caught watching?

replies.text: Me too! The Ashwarden caught me. They only looked. I have never felt so seen. I went home.
Then you are better at it than me, or you are not very interested. Both are good.

lines: Always. Remembrancer is my favourite. I write names in the ash with a stick, and scuff them out, and write them again, because they were wrong.
Ashwardens and Intruders. I am an Ashwarden. The Intruder is {neighbour}, and they are very bad at it. They keep waving. A good Intruder does not wave.
Lantern-keeper is a game with a string and a row of pebbles. Each pebble is a lantern. You say its name and move it. I have never lost a pebble. Except one. It rolled.
Brewery is mud and ash in a cup. You stir it and say it is a Mending. Nobody drinks it. It is the most useful pretend brew, because it is nothing at all.
