Wart-row is the one where you lie down between the rows. We are the wart. The grown-ups are the growers. They have to find us without stepping. They always step.
Bonecarver is hard to play, because you have no bone. We use a stick and pretend it is a rib. I carved a whole arch from one stick. It lasted until the stick broke.
My best game is Vigil. Everyone stands in a ring and says a name, any name, and someone has to guess who it is. Nobody is ever right. It is the best.
The grown-ups say we play at the same things they do. We do not. We play at the things they do when nobody is looking.

lines.text: I will tell you what I play when I know your face. Games are secret. Some of them are so secret even I do not know the rules.
If you play, you have to pick a job. You can be the stranger. That is a job. It is the best one, because you can ask questions all through the game.
I invented a game called Lost Outsider. You stand in the middle and are lost, and we all guide you. You must be very lost. Most people are not lost enough.
We tried playing Hollowed and Keepers with a toy skull from the Bonecarver once. It looked too real. The Remembrancer took it away. Now we play with a lantern instead.
I always play the one who gets it wrong, so everyone can say no, not like that. It is the most helpful job. The grown-ups should try it. They would learn so much.
I would like you to be in a game. Not as the stranger. As yourself. We would call it Visit, and the rule is that the visitor wins, because they came.
When I am grown I will play a game with you where I am the Remembrancer and you are the name on the Wall. It will be very solemn. Then we will have a warm cup.
Will you play? You can be the Intruder. It is the best job.

replies.text: Good! Walk in slowly. Do not wave. An Intruder never waves. *giggles* You waved.
Nobody is too old. I saw an Ashwarden hop over a crack in the lane once, when they thought the lane was empty.

lines.text: Do the grown-ups ever play?

replies.text: They do. They call it a rite. It has rules and nobody wins. Sounds like a game to me.
They do. They just call it something solemn first, and then do it anyway.

lines: We greet with a name. You give yours, I give it back, and now it has been heard twice. That is our whole system of manners. The rest is waiting politely.
We never blow out a candle. Breath is for names. Pinch the wick between two fingers, and thank it. The candle will not answer, but it will know.
Two fingers laid on the breastbone mean thank you, welcome and I am sorry. Context does the rest. Mostly context. Sometimes a long look.

lines.text: Outsiders break a custom within a few breaths of arriving. Do not worry. We write them down. It is a kind of attention.

replies.text: Careful is a fine custom. We have no word against it, and we have words against nearly everything.
The lantern chain, and the humming. We are keeping both, gently, like a pair of small, well-meant debts.
Habits are customs nobody is watching. Here, somebody always is.

lines: A question is answered on the second asking. It proves you meant it. Ask me twice, and I will tell you what I think of the custom.
We count in threes and say the third softer, for the Three. One, two, *Three*. It makes arithmetic solemn and quarrelling slow.

lines.text: Bone is never dropped, only set down, even a splinter. An outsider once tossed a rib over their shoulder. We stood very still until it was over.

lines: A gift is given with both hands and never wrapped. Wrapping hides, and we are suspicious of hiding. We have found too many things in too many sleeves.
On the lanes, walk left of the posts and keep your hand off the lantern chain. Each light is lit for someone, and you would not tug a person's sleeve.

lines.text: At a door, the younger holds it and says the name they keep, under their breath, the way you would clear your throat. It is not luck. It is habit.
We would rather say 'not yet' than 'late'. It is kinder, and only said of the living. The dead are never late. They are always exactly where we left them.
A thumb of ash across the brow is an oath. Break it, and we do not punish you. We only keep the ash, and let you see us keeping it. It is worse.

lines: Meals are quiet. At table the only words allowed are names and 'pass the wart'. Both are heard often, though not usually in that order.
We do not whistle in the lanes. A whistle is a note with nobody's name on it, and the Cairnbacks do not know where to put it.
Eyes down in the Hall of the Three, eyes up at the Name Wall. The Three ask for nothing. The names would like to see who is reading them.

lines.text: We do not point at the Hollowed, or at a lantern gone out. Pointing is for living things. We nod, slowly, as you would to a stranger at a funeral.
A new lantern joins the lane whenever the Vigil loses someone. The lane is longer than when I was small. The Remembrancer says that is not an accomplishment.
A friend may lay a hand on the Name Wall. A stranger may read it but not touch. I have never seen a friend's hand do harm, but the custom is old, and so are we.
When I trust someone, I tell them the one flaw of the name I keep. It is a custom. It says I know {kept} as they were, and not as a statue.
You say hello to every lantern on the lane, or it sulks. I say hello to all of them. It takes ages. {neighbour} only waves. Their lantern sulks.
You must not touch the Name Wall unless a grown-up is looking. If a grown-up is looking, you can touch it for a count of three. One, two, Three.
Two fingers on your chest means thank you. I do it for everything. The Brewer says I have thanked a pot of wart eleven times. It was a good pot.
Never blow out a candle! I did, once, at a Vigil. Everybody turned round. I will be sorry for a long time. It is a long list already.
At meals you say a name before you eat. I say all the ones I know. By then the wart is cold. Grown-ups say that is part of the custom.
I am not allowed to whistle in the lanes. I am allowed to hum, if it is a sad one. I know four sad ones. I know one that is not sad, but I keep it secret.
We have no festivals as outsiders mean them. We have Vigils, the Relighting, the Reaping and the Hush. Outsiders call them festivals because there is food afterward. They are right.
The Relighting: once a year every lantern on the lane is put out at once. We stand in the dark for a count of Three. Then the Cairnback walks the lane, and we light them again, one by one.

replies.text: So we remember what the lanterns are for. Every year someone trips, and every year it is the same lesson.
A little. That is rather the point. A light you have never lost is not a light, only a habit.
Time is the one thing we have to waste. We choose to waste it on the dark. Others waste it on gold.

lines.text: At the Relighting people hold hands, which they otherwise do not. It is the most affection we show all year, and we are embarrassed for a long while after.
At a Vigil there are three silences. Ashrin's is long. Velmir's is short. Thalys's is cut off in the middle, the way their life was. Nobody has ever finished it.
The Remembrancer reads the first name of a Vigil, and the youngest child who can read has the last. That is why our children practise their letters so hard. It is surprisingly competitive.
After the last name we eat, and nobody speaks, because mouths are full and names are heavy. It is the quietest feast in the Nether. Visitors always think something has gone wrong.
The Carrying: when someone dies, a new lantern is walked the whole length of the lane before it is hung. Everyone says the name as it passes. By the end even strangers know them.
A new name goes onto the Wall three ways: in ash, then in paint, then in stone. The Remembrancer says the ash is the real one. The rest is for people who do not trust ash.
The Reaping: the whole Vigil goes to the terraces and the wart is cut. After the last row we stand still and say sorry to the wart. It is our oldest apology, and the only one the wart accepts.
The Laying is a festival only because the whole Vigil attends. The sand takes the dead, and we say their name until the last grain has settled. It is long. It is the most honest thing we do.
The Hush is held when the Wall is full and a new stretch must be built. While the first block is laid, no one speaks. It may be the loudest festival we have.
Nobody dances. We walk in a line behind the Cairnback, slowly, in step. Outsiders say it is a funeral. We say it is dancing for people with a great deal on their minds.

lines: There is a song for the end of a Vigil. It has no words, only the low flute. The Cairnbacks seem to like it. At least they do not leave.

lines.text: Visitors may come to the Relighting if they stand at the back and bring their own candle. You are welcome. I will save you a place near a pillar, in case you trip.
At the last Vigil I said {kept}'s name aloud in the Hall, alone, with the Remembrancer nodding. Every keeper gets one turn. Mine was short. My hands shook anyway.
If you are here for the next Vigil, stand beside me. I will slip your name into the Saying between two others. Nobody will notice. I will.
For the Vigil I make a pale, weak brew that tastes of very little. It is meant to be forgettable, so that you remember the names. Most years I outdo myself.
The Relighting is my busiest time. Every wick, every chain, all set right within a count of Three. I dream of it. In the dream, I trip.
At the Reaping I cut the first row myself and leave the last uncut. The last row is for the wart to remember. It has not yet complained about the arrangement.
Before each Vigil I carve a small bone token for every child's first choosing. No two alike. They always lose them. I always carve more.
At the Relighting an Ashwarden stands at the Vigil's edge and counts to Three twice: once for the Vigil, once for whatever is outside. Nothing has ever answered.
The Vigil is my season of dread and joy. Every name read true, every letter checked. If I misread one, the Hall does not laugh. It is worse. It sighs.
My favourite is the Relighting! It gets so dark you can feel it. Then somebody giggles, and then everyone is trying not to. The Cairnback is the only quiet one.
At the Vigil you have to stay quiet for ages. I got to the middle once. The Remembrancer said that is a record for a small person.
There is a feast after the Vigil. I eat everything. Grown-ups say I eat like a Cairnback, slow but steady. I think that is a compliment.
At my first Vigil I get to walk the whole Wall alone, and every name will be looking at me. I practise standing very straight, so they can see I am serious.
I was asked to carry a lantern in the Carrying! I held it so carefully my arms shook for ages. The Lantern-keeper said I was the best lantern-carrier ever. They say that to everyone.
The Hush is boring and I love it. You cannot speak, so you look at everyone's faces, and everyone's faces try not to laugh. The Remembrancer always wins.

lines: I was a quiet child, which is no distinction here. I was a quiet child who hummed. The Remembrancer said they could find me by the gap in the silence.
I learned my letters in a tray of ash, with one finger. When you made a mistake, you shook the tray and began again. I did a great deal of shaking.
My first lantern chore was trimming one wick, once, with a Lantern-keeper watching. I trimmed it too short. The wick forgave me. The Lantern-keeper took a while.

lines.text: I stacked three bones once, only to see. Nothing happened. The Remembrancer's face happened. I have not stacked since. The face is a very good teacher.

replies.text: Long. Patient. The face of someone counting very slowly to a number they hoped never to reach.
So I thought. The Remembrancer asked whether I would like to be the one on the bottom. I have not thought it since.
No. I stacked wart instead. It rolled. There was a lesson in that as well, though a smaller one.

lines: We were sung the Counting Song, which is every name on the Wall, in order, to a tune. I was nine verses in before I understood they were people. I still hum it in the brewery.
I was told the Hollowed take loud children. It worked until I learned the Hollowed do not care how loud you are. Then I was loud on purpose, once. Then I was sorry.
My parent carved bone, and I was not allowed to touch the bench. I touched the bench. My parent made me carve a handle for it. I still have the handle.
I fell into a wart terrace once, face first. The growers were upset about the wart, then about me, in that order. I have never forgotten which came first.
We had a Cairnback when I was small, called Plod. I leaned on it for years. When it died I said its name for a long while, and nobody told me to stop.
At my first Vigil I walked the whole Wall three times before I chose. People were polite. By the third time they were very polite.
Children here are raised by the whole Vigil. If I did something wrong, six people knew before I did. If I did something right, six people said nothing. It was efficient.
I wanted to be an Ashwarden because of the circlet. The three sockets looked like small dark doors. Then I learned what they were for, and wanted to be a Brewer. Most of us do, eventually.
The first outsider I ever saw was a tall, loud shape at the valley's rim. I hid under a bench. It was only a Piglin, a long way off. I stayed under the bench anyway. It is a very good bench.
A child's first lie is to say they remember someone they never met. We forgive it. It is how every keeping begins.
At my first Vigil the whole Hall stood up. I thought it was for me. It was for the Three. I have never mentioned this to anyone until now.
The only thing I was ever punished for was talking in the Hall. They sat me beside the Cairnback. It listened. I stopped talking out of shame.
I used to count the lanterns from our doorstep and always got a different number. Either I counted wrong, or someone was being lit as I counted. I never knew which, and it was lovely.
My parent's way of saying they loved me was to trim my bedroll, corner by corner. I did not understand it then. I have thought about it a great deal since.

lines.text: I was the smallest at my first Vigil and the worst at silence. Now I keep the Wall. The Wall has a sense of humour, or I do. We have been together too long to tell.
I carved a toggle at nine. It looked like a skull. Most things do, the old Bonecarver said, kindly, and handed me a harder bone.
I learned lanterns by holding the ladder. For years I held the ladder. Then they gave me the wick. It was the best thing anyone has given me, and I told nobody.
My first row was crooked. The old grower walked it with me and said, wart does not mind crooked, it minds being stepped on. I have watched my feet ever since.
I spilled a pot on my first try at the bench. The Brewer said every good brewer has a ruined pot, and gave me the cloth. I have ruined many since. I am improving.
As a child I stood still to see how long I could. An Ashwarden found me, still standing, and said I had a gift. I took it as an instruction.
I will tell you a child's fear: that I would reach my first Vigil and find every name already chosen. They were not. The Wall had room. I was wrong, and lucky.
When I was small I told {kept}'s sign a secret, aloud, to its face. I have never told anyone what it was. But I told them first. That is part of why I chose them.

topics.ask: What do you eat and drink?
lines: Wart, mostly. Roasted, mashed, dried, ground to flour and baked. Wart bread is dense and faithful. It sits in you like a promise.

lines.text: Every meal begins with a spoonful put into the hearth for {kept}. It burns blue and small. They have never complained about the portions.
We leave one seat at a shared meal, with a bowl before it. The bowl is for no one in particular. Whoever is missed most at that meal may take it, silently.
We drink only brew. The one water in the Nether is what the Ghastkin cry, and we will not drink that. Grief cannot be a drink, and it takes the name away.
The ordinary brew is thin wart ale, brown and bitter. It tastes of the inside of a barrel. The Brewer says that is the point. The Brewer drinks very little of it.
Grey tea is wart skins steeped until they give up. It tastes of ash and apology. It is what I drink when I am sad. I am sad rarely. I drink it often, to be safe.
Sweets are rare. Candied wart is wart boiled in whatever sweetness the Brewer can find, which is usually none. It is candied in hope. It is still better than nothing, barely.
We eat no beast that carries a fire. A Cairnback is a lantern with legs, and you do not eat a lantern. It would also take ages.
Meat is a memory here. We eat what grows, and what has no name to keep. Wart has no name. It is the perfect food, and very nearly the only one.
Outsiders always ask what we eat. I think they hope for something worse. Wart, I say. They look relieved, then bored.

replies.text: Then you will do well here. Not many say that and mean it.
Thin ale, grey tea and the occasional candied thing. We call it a varied diet. Nobody has argued.
It is dull, and it is always there. Those two go together more often than outsiders expect.

lines: A good brew is like a good name. Said slowly, it warms you. Said too fast, you cough.

lines.text: Our only spice is blaze powder, a pinch at a time. Too much and the soup remembers it is fire. Too little and it remembers nothing, which is the usual trouble.
At the Vigil feast the soup is thin, so nobody can say they came for the soup. We came for the names. The soup is the apology.
We eat slowly. A meal is a way of staying in a room with people. When it is finished and nobody has left, we call it a good meal.
Leave nothing in a bowl, if you eat with us. A bowl left half full looks like an unfinished sentence, and we have enough of those.
I will cook for you, if you stay long enough. It is a wart stew. It is the best stew in the Nether, because it is the only one I have heard of.
A friend once set a seat for {kept} at their table, unasked. I could not eat much. I do not think I tasted a thing. It was the best meal of my life.
I brew the thin ale for the many and the dark tea for the few. The thin ale is a kindness. The dark tea is a punishment, which I give with love.
I know five ways to cook wart and a hundred ways to explain it. The best is split on soul-fire embers with a little ash. Eat the ash. It is part of it.
I eat standing at the bench, so the dust does not settle in my bowl. It settles in me instead. The bowl, at least, stays clean.
On duty we eat dry wart cake, one-handed, standing. It is not good. It is not meant to be. A guard who enjoys a meal is a guard who stops looking.
I fast before a Vigil to keep my head clear, and eat everything after to keep my head clear again. It all comes back to the head.
I eat out on the lane, a bowl on a post, so no lantern is ever left alone. The posts hear my worst table manners. They have never said a word.
I like wart porridge with ash on top. The ash is for crunch. The Brewer says it is for flavour. The Brewer is wrong. The ash is for crunch.
I am not allowed to lick the stirring paddle. I licked it. It was warm. It was also sour. Now I know both things and I wish I only knew the first.
There is a seat at meals that nobody sits in. I sat in it once. Everybody went quiet, and then {neighbour} gave me an extra helping. I think that was a punishment.
Candied wart is my favourite thing! It is sweet and a bit sad. Grown-ups say that is how all sweet things are.
I tried to eat something that was not wart once. It was a bone-meal pancake. It was terrible. Do not tell anyone I told you.
I drank the dark tea once. It tasted like when the lanterns go out. I did not finish. The Brewer said nobody does, and gave me a crumb of candied wart.
The valley is soul sand to the horizon, and the horizon is a ceiling of rock. We call the sand the Quiet, because it takes the sound of your steps and gives nothing back.
Soul sand holds on to your feet. It is not malice, but you could mistake it. It holds anything that stands still long enough to be remembered. A bit like us.
Along the valley wall run the Ribs: huge old bones set in the rock, from beasts older than any Wall. The Bonecarvers take only what falls. Nobody pulls one loose. That is the first rule of the Ribs.
The ghasts drift over us and cry, and sometimes throw fire at the terraces. We rebuild. We do not shoot back. They are our grief, and you do not shoot your grief.

replies.text: It is stubborn. It would take a great many arrows to hit all of it, and we are not a people for arrows.
They have. We said the names. We always say the names. It is not an answer, but it is the one we have.
We tried an answer once. It was called the Wither. I will take patience over another one, thank you.

lines.text: The sand shifts. Sometimes it gives back what it took: a toggle, a toy, a bone. We bring it to the Remembrancer, who puts it on the Shelf of Found Things. Nothing is claimed. The shelf is full.
There is a place called the Sink where the sand is so soft that things go in and do not come out. We do not go there. Each year we set a bone bead at its edge for whoever is under.

lines: The air hums, very low, like a flute breathed through a bone. Some say it is the souls. I say it is the wind in the Ribs. We both rest badly.

lines.text: No water, no trees, no birds. Whoever called it the Valley was being kind. The first Withren to name it called it the Place We Did Not Leave. It did not stick.

lines: The wart is the only red for a long way. When I am low I look at the terraces. They look back, in their way.

lines.text: In the valley we speak of places by who lies under them. Past Maret's Cairn. Left at Ostrin's Post. Our maps are lists of names. Outsiders get lost. Names, it turns out, are not directions.
From the top terrace you can see every lantern in {village} at once, a spill of blue along the dark. I stand there when I need to remember there are more of us than me.
Out here the sand is quieter than in a Vigil. No lanterns. You learn how much the lanterns do. Without them I must be the lantern. I am a poor one.
Beasts of the valley: Cairnbacks, ghasts overhead, a strider now and then on the far lava. Nothing that bites. Anything that bites is a Piglin, and they come from elsewhere.
The valley has no seasons and no hours. We make them: the Relighting, the Reaping, the Vigil. Without them everything would simply be.
If you cross the Grey Reach, the open sand, keep a hand on a lantern post until you cannot see the lane. After that, keep a hand on your name. Say it. It helps the sand know you are still someone.
My favourite place is the edge where the Ribs meet the sand. A long curve of bone like a hall for giants. I sit under it sometimes. It feels like being looked after by something I will never meet.
I will show you a place, if you come back. It is not on the lanes. It is where the sand is oldest and the wither roses grow best. I go there to speak to {kept} without the Wall between us.
Walking the lane I can tell the sand's mood by how the flames lean. Toward the Sink means it is hungry. Toward the Hall means it is calm. They have not yet lied to me.
Wart grows best where the sand is oldest. I have a row near the Ribs that yields twice the others. I do not ask why. I bring it extra patience and my best manners.
The Ribs give me my best bone. I go out when a piece falls, carry it back on a sled, and thank the gap it leaves. The gap has not yet answered.
From my post I watch the open sand. Nothing moves there for a long while. Then something does. In between, I am very good at nothing.
The valley is so big! Bigger than my house, bigger than the Hall, bigger than everything. Grown-ups say it is even bigger than that. I think they are trying to scare us.
I found a bead in the sand once! The Remembrancer put it on the Shelf of Found Things. I visit it. Sometimes I say hello, in case it was someone's.
Do not step off the lanes! The sand eats shoes. Mine went last year. I got them back, but they were different. They were more patient.
The ghasts cry all the time. I think they miss someone. I say sorry from the doorstep, but I do not think they hear me. I will try louder.
My favourite thing in the whole valley is the Ribs. They look like the oldest cage in the world, with nothing inside it. It makes me feel big for fitting.
I am not allowed past the last lantern. I went three posts past once. An Ashwarden stood in my way and said nothing. It was the loudest nothing.
A Remembrancer and a Brewer walk into a room and everyone stops talking. This is not a joke. It is simply what happens.
The dead make the best listeners and the worst conversation. They are, however, excellent at being right. Nobody has ever contradicted them.
I asked an Ashwarden to smile on duty. They said the circlet was too heavy. I said the circlet is empty. They said, that is why.

lines: The funniest creature in the valley is a Cairnback trying to be late. It cannot. It has never been anywhere early enough to be on time.

lines.text: It takes seven Withren to light one lantern. One lights it, and six remember to say the name afterward. We are very thorough, and it is very slow.

lines: We have a proverb: a stacked skull is a short lesson. We have another: do not.

lines.text: The wart-growers say wart grows because they talk to it. They do not say it also grows when they leave. Growers say very little.
A visitor asked whether Withren ever laugh. I said, only after someone has left. It is the polite time.
Our bedrolls are very comfortable. We know this because nobody has ever told us otherwise, and the alternative goes off like a ghast.
Ask a Bonecarver for a funny carving and they will make a skull. Ask again and they will make a smiling skull. A skull is always smiling. That is the joke.
The Remembrancer has an excellent sense of humour. They keep it in a drawer, in order. I have been laughing at the same joke for years. I find it only improves.

lines: An outsider once bowed to a Cairnback. It did not bow back, but it took a very long time not to.

lines.text: I do not tell jokes at the Wall. I tell them near it, quietly, in case someone wants one. A name laughed near is a name loved. I think. I am still testing it.
We are told we are gloomy. We are not gloomy. We are punctual about grief. The rest of the time we are quite cheerful, and keep it under a hood.

replies.text: Thank you. Nobody does. I have decided to find that funny, and I do, a little.
Then we are succeeding at the hood. It is a good hood.
*a very small, very careful smile* There. That was the whole of it. It cost me a good deal.

lines.text: You have a funny walk. Heavy, certain and alive. I do not mean it unkindly. It is the walk of someone the Wall has never looked at, and it makes me smile.
I told this to the Wall and it laughed, or a draught moved. A Withren asks the Wall for a place for their name. The Wall says: eleven from the bottom, near a draught. Even the dead get complaints.
Dry humour is the only humour that keeps. Wet humour spoils, and we have no water. That is our whole theory of comedy. I have never been wrong. I have also never been funny.
Brewer's joke: what is the difference between a medicine and a poison? The label. Nobody has read the label since the War.
Ask a Lantern-keeper how many wicks they trimmed and they say 'a few'. Ask again and they say a number. Ask a third time and they weep. It is the oldest joke we have.
Why do wart-growers never gossip? Wart is an excellent listener. It never repeats a word, and it never tires of hearing the same one.
An Ashwarden's idea of a joke is to stand silently in your way and then step aside very slowly. I have caused three laughs this way. Each was a cough.
I remember every joke ever told in this Vigil. That is why I am rarely invited to meals. My jokes are mostly yours, repeated at the wrong time.
The Cairnback has been halfway across the lane since the last Vigil. It is thinking about the other half. That is the joke. {neighbour} says it is not a joke. It is, it just takes ages.
I put a hood on the Cairnback. It stood there all through the Hush and looked very serious. Everybody said it looked like a little Remembrancer. I got in trouble, but it was worth it.
Why do Withren never get lost? Because we always remember where we are going. Also we never go anywhere. Same thing.
When I grow up I am going to be a Remembrancer who forgets everything. Then everybody has to tell me their names again and again. I will make so many friends.
Do you want to hear a joke about the Wall? I have not got one. But the Wall is listening, so I said I did. Now we are all waiting. Wait with me.
I told the Ashwarden a joke. They did not smile, but their eyebrow moved. That means they loved it. Nobody has ever got an eyebrow before.

lines: Nobody alive fought in it, but we all inherited it, like a family nose or a family debt. Ours is the debt. We pay it in names.
The old people say it began when a Piglin dug under a terrace and found our dead where the gold should have been. It is too neat to be true. I tell it anyway.
My family's story: we lost three in the War. One at a door, one at a bridge, one nobody can find. The one nobody can find, we say twice.
The old word for a soldier was 'wick', meant to burn short and bright. The soldiers used it themselves, bitterly, then fondly. It is still an insult. It is also a title.

lines.text: The gold itself was never ours. It lay under the sand where our dead were laid, and a thing under the dead is not a treasure. It is a grave with a glint.

replies.text: They wanted a life with a floor of gold under it. I understand that. I would not have dug through my parent's grave to get it.

replies.ask: Could you not have shared it?
replies.text: It lay under our dead. You cannot share a grave with someone who means to melt it down.
So is a knife. It is what you do with it, and what it does to you.

lines: Piglin war-bands left their own where they fell. We went out after the fighting and said names over them, any names. The Piglins called it witchcraft. We called it the least we could do.
The Wall's old records say the Weft took bone from our dead for needles. Some say only what was left on the field. The records say it was not only. We believe the records.
There is a song about the Last Answer that nobody sings. We all know it. We hum the tune on the way to the terraces and stop before the end. It is our oldest custom, stopping.
Everyone's grandparent told a different story of the Wither. In some it was blue. In some it roared. In one, which I believe, it was very quiet, and drifted as if it were sorry.
The Magmari ferried the Piglins. The Weft took our bones. The Piglins dug. Everyone did a part, so no one did it. That is how we hold the War: as a thing everyone had a hand in.
The Wall says {kept} held a door. I think of the door when I stand at the Vigil's gate. I am holding it for them now. The gate does not need holding. I do.
There were many more Vigils before the War. There are few now. The rest are only lists. I count them when the lanterns burn low, and it does not help.
The Hall of the Three was built after the Last Answer, not before. We did not honour them while they lived. We asked, they answered, and then we built a hall. I think about the order of those things.
Children are told the War in three parts, one for each of the Three. The last part is always the shortest. Thalys's. The elders stop early and let the silence finish it.
There are fortresses we cannot enter, because the Hollowed hold them. In the Wall's records they are listed like graves. They are graves with doors.
A wanderer told me the Piglins sing about the War too. I asked what the song is like. 'Loud,' they said, 'and the gold is in every verse.' We have a verse about gold too. It is: do not.
Everything I know of the Piglins I learned from the War. Everything I know of the War I learned from the Wall. Everything I know of the Wall I learned from an old Remembrancer who knew nothing else.

lines.text: The ones who made the Last Answer were not villains. They were tired, cornered and brave, and no wiser than we are. I remember that when someone says we would never do it again. We might.
When I say the Three's names I try to hear the room they left. It is the same size as the room I would leave. I find that helpful and dreadful in turn.
If the War ever came again, I think I would say no. I think. I have thought about it for years and the answer is still 'I think'. I hope it is never tested.
I would not let the Three go alone, if it came to it. I say this to no one. Say it to the Wall, if you must. I would stand beside them. I would be useless. I would stand.
We Ashwardens are said to descend from the war guards. The ribs on our chests are not decoration. They are an oath: never again guard against the wrong thing.
The records of the War are the longest in the tower. I read them once a year and weep once a year. It balances. The records do not mind.
A few lanterns on the lane are lit for war dead nobody can name. I tend those first. They never go out. They have had practice.
The oldest carving in the Vigil is a door from the War, with no one behind it. I oil it every few years. It does not need it. I do.
In the War a Brewer's work was to make the pain stop, not to win. We still say a Brewer's name softly in the Hall, as you would a healer's.
Wart fed the Vigils through the War. The Piglins thought it worthless and left the terraces alone. It was the one time we were glad to be underestimated.

lines: I have loved twice. One is on the Wall now, and someone else keeps them. The other I can see from my door. I will not say which I think of more.
We do not say 'I love you'. We say your name when we are alone, which is rare, and that is the same thing. It is also cheap. A name costs nothing and means everything.
To court a Withren, bring a candle and sit near them, silent, for as long as they allow. Not a word. If they leave it burning, you have been heard.
Two Withren share a wick: they light one lantern between them, say both names and both keepings, and carry it down the lane together. It is slower than it sounds. It is the whole of a wedding.
Two who share a wick always keep different names, and each thinks the other's is more interesting. I keep {kept}, who has no famous anything. I like to think I won.
Love is remembering someone when you have no need to. That is why we keep the dead so well. They ask for nothing, and we give them everything. It is practice for loving the living.
A child's parents love them the way anyone loves what they will one day have to say the name of. It is not cold. It is the kind of love that knows what it is for.

lines.text: When a child is born, the Remembrancer reads the Wall to them, all of it, while they sleep through it. It is the longest welcome in the Nether. They wake knowing everyone and meet no one.

lines: I loved someone who left for another Vigil. It is rare, and it hurts like a death with a face. I send a lantern at the Relighting. I do not know if it arrives.
If a loved one dies, you cannot keep them when you already keep another. Someone else chooses them. You visit the sign and ask whether they are said enough. They always are. It is somehow worse.
The strangest thing about love is that it fits in the same breast as grief. I carry both. The Wall says there is room.
There is a love unrelated to partners: the love of the Vigil itself. The lane at its quietest, the light on the Wall. It is the only love that never asks you to stay. It only asks you to look.

lines.text: To be loved by a Withren, be consistent. We do not ask for passion. We ask for the same face, at the same door, for many years. That is the highest compliment.

replies.text: That is all anyone has asked, for a long time. Thank you.
It is. It is also the most restful thing in the Nether. Try it before you judge.
Then we will say your name more. It is the Withren way of being furious.

lines: A love letter here is a list of the names you have said for someone. If it is long, you have been loved. If your own name is in it, you have been loved a great deal.
I have heard that outsiders press their faces together to show fondness. I would like to see this, from a respectful distance, with a Cairnback in front of me.
We are not romantic. We are devoted. It is a different thing. Romance is a candle; devotion is the wick. I am told other peoples are better at the first. I am told it burns out quicker.
I am told the Piglins love loudly and the Magmari love by haggling. We love by remembering. It is the quietest of the three and, I think, the one that leaves the most behind.

lines.text: Sharing a wick need not mean partners. Two friends can do it. I did, once, long ago. If we are ever in the Hall together, I might ask you. Do not answer at once. I will need time to stop shaking.
We have a word for a friend who stays: a long wick. You are one. It is not a compliment. It is a description. A long wick burns slowly, gives steady light and does not ask for much.

I have been asked for a love potion. I brew a thin ale and say, drink this slowly with the person in question. It has worked eleven times. The twelfth, they married the wrong person. The ale was fine.
For each pair who share a wick I carve matching toggles, with a small mark on the inside where only they can see. I never tell anyone what the mark is. I never tell myself.
When two share a wick, I tend that lantern for the rest of their lives. I know their names better than I know my own. It is an odd intimacy, and I treasure it.
A pair of growers plant two rows side by side at the same time. If both thrive, it is a good match. If one fails, we blame the soil. Always the soil.
An Ashwarden's love is done on duty: two posts, one lane, a nod now and then. It is not much. It is enough to build a life on.
Being a Remembrancer is a poor way to be loved. You remember everything about a person, and they hate it. I have been left four times for knowing how they would begin their sentences.

lines: We seldom meet. The Piglins keep to their Holds, the Magmari to their lava, the Weft to their trees, the Ghastkin to their pillars. A meeting is an event. It is usually a bad one.
Once a year a Piglin hunting party crosses the valley's edge, in gold, shouting. We stand still and wait until they are bored. A Withren can stand still longer than any Piglin can shout.

lines.text: A Magmari barge drifted close once, and the Magmari aboard called out a price for the view. The Ashwarden answered, 'None.' The barge moved off. It was the longest talk we have had with a Magmari.

lines: A Weft rope-walker once crossed the valley edge, bright as a lantern, four arms and not a word. We watched them cross. They watched us watch. Nobody breathed until they were gone.
A Ghastkin came to the edge of the Vigil once, weeping softly. The Ashwardens did not ask why. It stood a while, said something I missed, and drifted off. We were relieved, and ashamed of it.
A stranger at the Vigil's edge is met by an Ashwarden, a bench and three questions. Who are you? What do you want? Whom do you keep? Most are done by the second.

lines.text: Nobody has answered the third question the same way twice. A Piglin says 'my gold'. A Magmari says 'my chain'. A Weft says 'my row'. A Ghastkin has not decided. It is a very good test.

replies.text: Then you are a rare sort of stranger. The bench is yours. We will see what you keep, in time.
A fine answer, and an honest one. It is the first time I have heard it. Sit down.
Because it is the first thing a stranger lies about, and the last thing they can.

lines.text: I have never hated anyone from another people. I have disliked a great many by name. This may be the same thing. Only the Remembrancer would know.

lines: The Piglins say Withren never smile. They have never seen us outside a Vigil. We smile at wart, and sometimes at each other, when we think nobody is looking. Please do not look.
A rumour went round that a Piglin and a Withren had shared a meal at the Vigil's edge. It was untrue. The meal was a rumour too.
Piglins sometimes steal from our terraces. They think wart is a kind of gold. They bite it raw and make a face we will be quoting for years.
Lost wanderers from other peoples knock on our posts maybe twice a year. We give them a bench, a cup of thin ale and directions home. Then we say their name, if they gave it. It is only manners.
An Ashwarden party takes a lantern to the nearest fortress each Relighting and sets it at the gate. It is never taken. It is never put out. Nobody talks about it. Everybody knows.
I would like to meet a Withren from a far Vigil one day. Vigils do not visit, mostly for the lava between. We hear of them from wanderers, write their Vigil names on a list, and hope.
The Piglins are the only ones who talk about their dead aloud. They boast about them, loudly, as if the dead might overhear and be pleased. I find it more touching than I would say.
I once saw a Ghastkin child and a Withren child stand either side of a basalt ridge, staring at each other. Neither moved. Neither spoke. Then both ran home. I hear it was the best meeting in years.

lines.text: If you meet a Piglin, wear your gold. If you meet a Magmari, bring a haggle. If you meet a Weft, count your fingers after. If you meet a Ghastkin, hold your name tight. If you meet us, just be you.
The peoples might get on if each cooked for the others. Nothing breaks a grudge like a bad meal shared. I told the Remembrancer. They called it the stupidest idea they had heard, and wrote it down.
You are a person of no people, who comes to each of us and listens. That makes you a threshold. Take care. A threshold is where every draught meets.
If you carry a message between us and any other people, I will not ask what it says. I will only ask you to carry it kindly. The message itself we can argue about for another hundred years.
I stand at the post and watch for strangers. Nearly all are lost. A few are not. I treat them all the same until I can tell. Kindness as a precaution is the hardest part of the job.
Strangers always ask about the lanterns. I tell them each one is lit for someone, and they go quiet. It works on every people. Even Piglins put their gold away.
I offer thin ale to wanderers. Most refuse. A Magmari once accepted and asked the price. 'Free,' I said. 'Then it is worthless,' they said, and drank it anyway.
A Piglin once tried to trade me gold for wart. I said, you may not have it. They said, a great deal of gold. I said, you may not have a great deal of it. They left in a state of confusion.
I keep a ledger of every stranger who came to the post, with the name they gave. Most are false. I write them down anyway. A false name said to the Wall is still said.
A Weft once asked to buy a bone from my bench. I said it was not for sale. They said everything is. I said, not this. We both knew what they wanted it for. They left. I carved nothing for a while.

lines: I fear the Wall running out of room, and then I remember we build more Wall. What I fear is that nobody will want to build it. A people that stops adding names has stopped being a people.
I fear the moment I say {kept}'s name and feel nothing. Not forgetting. Worse: saying it by habit, like a latch. I try to say it differently each time, to keep the latch from rusting.
I fear the Hollowed less than what they show. They were whole, and then they were not. If it can happen to a fortress full of Withren, it can happen to anyone who stops paying attention.

lines.text: I fear a new Wither. Not the ones outsiders make; those are woken and can be killed. I fear that one day someone with a clear voice will say 'we need an answer', and I will agree.

replies.text: Perhaps not. I would like to be sure. That is why I say it aloud, to friends, at length.
Please do. Bring a Cairnback. They are very good at slowing things down.
Maybe. That is exactly what the last ones said. Be careful what you agree to quickly.

lines: I fear silence that is not chosen. The Hush is a gift. The silence after you call a name and nobody answers is another thing. I have no words for it. That is the whole fear.
I fear the lanterns going out all at once, not at the Relighting, but truly. I dream of the dark that lasts. I rise and check the lane. The lane is always lit. I check again.
I fear being a bad keeper. Not wicked, just bored. What if {kept} deserved someone who loved the work? I try to be fascinated. It is hard to be fascinated by someone you never met.
I fear the sky. Not the ceiling, the ghasts beneath it. A Withren looks up so rarely that I am afraid of everything above me, and have never told it.
I fear the Sink, and I fear that I do not fear it enough. The sand has no interest in me. That is the most dangerous kind of interest.
I fear outsiders who do not look at the Wall. They stand before it and look past it, as if names were scenery. I fear what they would do with a skull, if names are scenery.
I fear that I am dull. A Withren can be dull in a very dignified way and never notice. I asked {neighbour}, who said I am not dull, I am Withren. I did not find that comforting.

lines.text: I fear the Remembrancer's death. They hold more names than anyone, and carry half of them in their head. If they go before it is all written down, a part of the Wall goes dark. We are writing fast.

lines: I fear a bed. I fear the bedroll less, and check it before I lie down. I do not know why. I know exactly why. It is the one fear I can make jokes about.
I fear the Weft's needles more than their fists. A fist is honest. A needle was once someone's bone, and it goes in clean.
I fear Ghastkin tears. One drop and the name goes. I fear I would not even notice. That is the fear: the thing taken, and the one who would have noticed, taken together.
I am afraid of how much I love this place. It is a hard place, and I am fond of it. If something took it, I would not know what to do with all that fondness.
I fear the end of a Vigil. The last name is said, the Hall empties, and I feel great relief. Then I feel guilty about the relief. Relief and guilt are a pair now. I keep them both.

lines.text: I fear being kept badly. I asked the Remembrancer who would keep me. They said I will find out in time. I am told this is meant to be comforting.
I fear that, asked as the Three were asked, I would have said yes. I do not know whether that is courage or only being polite.
My deepest fear is that you will go, and I will be a name you once heard. I know that is not how it works. I know it. That is why I am telling you.
I fear blight. A single grey row can sour a terrace by the next Vigil. I watch the leaves the way you would watch a stranger's hands.
I fear the moment a lantern goes out and I do not know whose it was. The Wall always tells me. I fear the day it does not.
I fear carving a living face by mistake. We carve only the dead. I check the Wall before every toggle. Twice. Then I carve something else, in case.
I fear the wrong potion in the wrong cup. I label everything twice, in two hands. I still go back to the bench, long after I have lain down, to check.
I fear the day I let in someone who should have been turned away. The post does not forgive, and neither do I. So I look at everyone as if they might be that person.
I fear misremembering a name aloud in the Hall, and nobody correcting me because they are too kind. Please correct me, if I do. I would rather be embarrassed than wrong.
I hope the Hollowed will one day have names. Not to bring them back. To say. A name said over a Hollowed is a small door opened. I hope it is enough.
I hope to finish my work before I finish. Not the work they give me, the work I give myself. There is a carving, a row, a list. I hope the list is shorter than I fear.
I hope to be kept by someone who would have liked me. That is all. The Remembrancer says it is the most common wish on the Wall, and the most commonly granted.
I hope the Vigil gets more children. A lane with no small footsteps is a lane waiting. A child is a lantern with legs.
I hope the five peoples find something to be ashamed of together. Shame shared is the best glue. It may be all we have.
I hope to see the Overworld before I go. Just the sky. I am told it is high, and I have a notion it is blue. I would say a name up at it. A person should say a name at the sky at least once.
I hope a Nether Star is brought to the Hall in my lifetime. The right way: carried gently, laid down. I hope whoever brings it knows what they are carrying.
I hope the ghasts overhead stop crying, and I hope nobody stops them. Both at once. It is a very Withren hope.
I hope someone will keep {kept} after me. I have been careful to be interesting about them, so that a child will want the job.
I hope for a better brew. Always. The Brewer says it will come. The Brewer has said so since I was small. The Brewer is still hoping.
I hope this lane lasts. I hope the lanterns stay lit, and the sand lets go of the right things and holds on to the right things. I hope all the small hopes that go with them.
I hope an outsider will one day ask me to teach them the Counting Song, and stay to the end. Verse thirty-nine. Nobody has ever stayed for verse thirty-nine.
I hope for a long, boring life. Nothing in the valley, nothing on the Wall, nothing at the post. A wart row that grows, a lane that stays lit. We are rarely lucky enough to be bored.
I hope the Magmari forgive us, and we forgive the Magmari. I hope it happens in the right order, so neither of us has to go first. It will take a very patient ferry.

replies.text: Yes. I have thought it might be me. I have not yet found the courage, only the hope.
They may not. I would still like to have asked. It is a small hope, and it can be carried on a very small boat.
The ferries carried it. Those are different verbs, and I have been trying to hold them apart.

lines.text: I hope you will come when I am old and the Wall is long. I hope you will bring someone and say my name, and say: this is who I came to see. That is all I want from a friendship.
I hope never to use what I have trained for. That is the whole of an Ashwarden's hope. Every year I do not draw my weapon is a victory.
I hope to light one more lantern than I put out. If every Lantern-keeper in history managed it, the Nether would be bright.
I hope to carve one thing so well that nobody knows it was carved. A bone that looks as though it grew that way. I am close. The Wall says I am not.
I hope for one terrace so perfect I do not want to touch it. I hope to see it once and then not touch it. The hope is easy. The not touching is hard.
I hope the next Remembrancer has a better memory and a worse sense of humour. A good memory is useful. A sense of humour is a liability.
I hope for one brew that comforts without making anyone forget. It is harder than it sounds. Most things that ease grief take the name with them. I keep trying.
I hope I choose right! When I walk the Wall I want the right name to light up like a lantern. Grown-ups say it does not, but I am going to keep hoping, in case.
I hope I get a Cairnback of my own. A small one. It could walk with me to the Hall, very slowly. We would get there in time for the next Vigil.
I hope the ghasts stop being sad. I would give them one of my lanterns if I could throw that high. I cannot. I am going to learn.
I hope to see the sky, the real one, where outsiders live. I think I would say hello to it. Probably very quietly. Probably it would not answer.
I hope you keep coming back! It is my biggest hope, bigger than the Cairnback. Do not tell the Cairnback.
I hope I get a good name to keep. Not too hard, not too sad. A funny one, if possible. I would make them laugh, even on the Wall.
I know your world from rumour, and from outsiders who talk too much. There is a sky, they say, with a lamp in it that nobody lights. I find that hard to believe. And yet, here you are.
Outsiders speak of 'rain': water falling out of nothing, on purpose. I cannot picture it. Is it unkind? Do you stand in it? Do you say a name at it? I would.
You have graves, I hear, in the ground, with stones. We lay ours in the sand, which is a stone grown soft. We are not so different. The difference is whether anyone says the name.
Your skeletons burn in your sunlight, they say. I hope it is quick. I do not think they are ours, but a skull is a skull, and I do not like to hear that one burns.
Your villages, do they keep names? Not of the dead. Of the living. I hear they trade with a nod and a strange green stone. It sounds like prayer to me.
You sleep in beds, which is the strangest thing I know about you. You lie on a thing that does not burst. You trust it. I would like to trust a bed once, from a long way off.
I am told your dead walk about in the dark and moan. Ours walk too, only they are the Hollowed, and they do not moan. They simply continue. I think we win the grim contest.
I have heard of grass. A green thing. It grows without a name. I think the Weft would like it. I think the Withren would not, because it would be too cheerful to keep.
A whole sea of water, to drink or to drown in. We have lava seas out beyond the valley. It seems a fair exchange. I cannot decide which is the more dangerous.
Do you have a Name Wall? A place where your dead are listed? If you do, you are halfway to us. If you do not, you would find it useful. It is not hard to build. The hard part is remembering.
The creatures you keep in pens, I am told, give milk and wool and eggs. We have the Cairnbacks. They give light. It is a different kind of milk.
Your world has doors that close and stay closed. Ours have doors that someone holds. I think that explains a good deal about us both.
I have heard of a land called the End, past the edge of your world. It is not yours and not ours. I hope it keeps its names. I expect it does. Something always does.
Do your people have a word for what you feel when a lantern goes out? I am told you have a word for everything except what matters.
Tell me one thing about your world that I would not guess. Do not tell me the sky. I have guessed the sky.

replies.text: Fields. No ceiling above and no wall beside. I have to sit down. Thank you. I am sitting down now.

replies.ask: We die where we were born.
replies.text: Then you are closer to us than I thought. We should compare Walls.
For fun. Well. I will not say what I think. I will say it to the Wall, and the Wall will tell you.

lines.text: If I came to your world, I would not know where to put my eyes. Up, mostly. I would be overwhelmed. The Remembrancer says I would be fine. The Remembrancer has never been.
I would like you to tell me your dead. Not the names, the stories. I will keep a few. I cannot keep them as mine, but I can keep them as yours. That is a smaller thing, and a true one.
When you go back to your world, say my name once to something that cannot answer. A tree. A hill. The sky. It does not have to know. I will.
I hear your brewers use a stand and a flame and a bottle, and no patience at all. I would give a great deal to watch one work. I would also give a great deal not to taste it.
They say your crops grow in light and water and ripen in no time at all. I cannot imagine a crop in a hurry. Ours grows at the pace of memory. Yours must be exhausting.
Do you have lanterns? Your sun must be a great one. Who trims it? Is there a ladder? I think about this more than I should, for a Lantern-keeper.
Do you have valley bone in your world, from beasts no one kept? I would trade a good deal for one rib to hold, just to know the weight.
I am told your world has soldiers who guard doors against the dark. I would like to meet one. I think we would stand side by side for a very long time, say nothing, and part friends.
I have heard your people write on paper, which burns. I do not understand how you trust it. Our names are in stone and in ash, and even then we worry. You must be very brave.
Is the sky really not a ceiling? I asked the Remembrancer, and they said 'It is higher.' I said how much higher, and they said 'Much.' That is no help!
Do you have Cairnbacks where you live? Or something that carries a fire on its back? I would like to meet it. I would walk very slowly the whole way.
They say there is a big bright lantern in your sky that never goes out. How does the Lantern-keeper trim the wick? I want to know more about this.
Do your grown-ups tell you to be quiet? Mine do. I think I would like your world, if it is loud. Is it loud?
Can I ask you a secret question? Do you have beds that do not burst? I have never lain on one. I would lie there and see what happens. I would be very brave.
I want to see rain. I have heard it is water that falls down on purpose. I would stand in it. I would get wet. I do not know what wet is but I want to know.

loved.text: Oh. This is very good. I will tell {kept} about it. They will be pleased for me, in their way.
For me? Really? I am going to show everyone. Then I am going to hide it so nobody takes it.

loved: You knew. Someone told you, or you guessed. Either way, I will remember this. That is not a small promise, here.
This goes by the hearth, where I keep the things that matter. There is not much room. I am making some.
*holds it a long moment* Thank you. Truly. The dead give no gifts, so we notice the living ones.

loved.text: Wart, freely given. I know what it cost to grow. The terraces thank you, and so does my stomach, which has a louder voice.
A wither rose. They grow only where something has ended, and they do not pretend otherwise. I will plant this by the Wall, where it will be understood.
A soul lantern. Who is it lit for? No, you need not say. I will hang it for the next name that has none, and tell them you sent it.
A soul campfire. A fire that keeps nobody warm and everybody company. I will set it where the lane bends and the dark is thickest.
A Hollowed skull. You carried it gently, and I will keep it gently. It goes to the Hall, set apart, never stacked. Thank you for treating it as though it still mattered.
Three souls, fused, and you bring them here. *a long silence* I cannot thank you enough, so I will thank you slowly, over many visits. This is the first.
A star! It is glowing! May I hold it? No? Then I will hold the hem of your coat. It is nearly as good.
I will say your name at the hearth when I next light it. You will have to take my word for it. That is what a promise is, here.
{kept} would have loved this. I will tell them, in a quiet moment. They keep quiet very well.

loved: I was not expecting kindness at this size. I shall have to sit down. Then I shall have to stand up again and look pleased.

loved.text: From you? This will not go on a shelf. It will go in my pocket, then on my bench, and when I die, on the Wall beside my sign. Someone will wonder why. Good.
It is the best thing anyone has ever given me. I know I said that about the last one. This one is better. I have a system.
Oh! It is glowy, or shiny, or something. I cannot tell, I am too happy. Wait, I have to show the Cairnback.
A brewer collects gifts to remember what it is to receive. I shall steep this one in thought. Not literally. Possibly literally.
I will carve a small thing in return. You will not know when. That is how a Bonecarver says thank you: the bone takes its time.
I will trim every wick on the lane a little finer for this. The light will be better. You will not notice. That is the gift I give back.
Wart-growers rarely get gifts. People think we have everything. We have wart. It is a great deal of wart. This is better.
I will mark this on my stole, beside the hopeful mark I keep for you. It is a small mark, but I read my stole whenever I need to feel rich.
An Ashwarden does not smile on duty. I am looking at the lane very hard so that you cannot see me failing.
You gave without being asked, and I took without a flinch. Do you know how hard that is for me? This is why you are Kept. Nobody else has ever managed it.

liked.text: Thank you! I know just where it goes. Well. I know where it does not go, which is a start.

liked: A good gift. Useful and quiet, like a good guest.
Thank you. I will use it well, and not wastefully. Waste is a kind of forgetting.
Ah. We have a place for this. We have a place for most things. Now it has one.
Kindly done. I will mention it at the hearth. Briefly. We do not gush. This is me gushing.

liked.text: A bone. I will assume it is a beast's and ask no questions, and you will offer no answers, and we shall both be comfortable. Thank you.
A block of bone, tidy and square. Whoever packed it was patient. I will give it to the Bonecarver, who will pretend not to care and then not leave the bench.
Bone meal. The growers swear it settles the soil, though wart takes no feed from it. It makes the terrace feel looked after, and wart notices.
A skull. Not one of ours, I think, but a skull is a skull. I will set it where nothing is stacked on it and say a name over it. Any name will do. It has not yet been picky.
A soul torch. Small, blue and honest. I will put it where the wick keeps failing on the lane. It will be an improvement, or at least a discussion.
A candle. Small gifts are the best kind. They burn down and ask to be given again. I will not blow it out. I will pinch it, and say thank you.
Soul sand, from your own pocket. It holds on to things, the old growers say. I hope it holds on to your good intentions and lets go of the bad.
Soul soil. It is quieter than sand, and it forgives the foot. The lanes are made of it. You are, in a small way, paving.
Basalt. Grey, cool and sure of itself. I like that in a guest as much as in a gift.
Polished basalt. Someone worked this smooth with patience; I can tell by the shine. I will use it for a name, and the name will be grateful.
A book. Blank or full, either is welcome. A blank book is a name waiting, and a full one is a Vigil someone else has already finished.
A book to write in. I will fill it with names in a small hand, and keep it beside the Wall's own. The Remembrancer will frown. Then borrow it.
A glass bottle. Empty, which is the best state for a bottle. A brewer's heart lifts at one. Mine lifts a little, and it is not even my bench.
Blaze powder. A spark in a pinch. We use it carefully, since fire and Vigil do not agree. I will keep it for the next brew that needs a nudge.

liked: Thank you. I will find a place for it, and the place will find me later, as places do.

liked.text: I like it! I am going to put it somewhere safe. Then I will forget where. Then I will find it, and be happy twice.
A brewer's shelf is never full. It is only never empty. This will go behind the good bottle, where I can see it and nobody else can.
Good. I can use this at the bench. Do not tell the children; they will want some.
You are learning what we like. It is not hard. It is only quiet. But you did it without being told, and that is the part I keep.
Thank you. We are strangers, and you bring me something I might have chosen. Either you are lucky or you are paying attention. I hope the second.

neutral: Thank you. I am not sure what it is for, but I will keep it. Keeping is the one thing we are good at.
A gift. Well. It is the giving we remember, mostly. The thing itself can be odd.
I will find a use for this. If not, I will find someone who has one. Nothing is wasted in a Vigil.
Hm. Thank you. *turns it over slowly* I will think about this one.
A strange thing. I will keep it by the door for a while and see whether it tells me what it is.
I do not know this, but I know it was meant kindly, and that is most of what a gift is.
It has no name I can see. I will give it one. Something small and safe. Something we can both live with.

neutral.text: Thank you. I will ask the Bonecarver whether it can be carved, and the Brewer whether it can be brewed. Between them, everything has a use.

neutral: I have no use for this, and I will find one. That is a way of being grateful, I think: finding a use for what you cannot use.

neutral.text: What is it? Is it a toy? A tool? A secret? Whatever it is, it is mine now, and I will name it. Its name is Gift.
It is not shiny and it is not bone. But it is new! I will put it with the other new things. There are three of them.
I will check whether it dissolves. If it does, we will learn something. If it explodes, we will learn something quicker.
Not bone, not stone. A mystery. I will hold it up to the light and wait for it to confess.
I will find a post for it on the lane. If it is not a lantern, it can at least keep one company.
I will bury it at the edge of the terrace and see what the wart makes of it. Wart is a good judge.
I must check this against the post's list of safe things. It is short. The list of safe people is shorter, and you are on it.
I will record it: giver, gift, and what it might be. I cannot guess the last, so I will write 'a gift' and let a later Remembrancer discover the rest.
I do not know you well enough to know what this means. I will take it as a good sign. Come again, and we shall both understand more.
You know I like useful things, and you know I like odd ones, so you chose one that is neither. I find that very endearing.
Whatever it is, it came from you, and that makes it worth more than itself. I will find it a shelf near the ones I love.

neutral: A gift of no particular colour. The best kind. It does not demand an opinion.
Thank you. I will make a place for it. That is how I welcome anything: first I make a place. The thing can follow.

neutral.text: Out here I will carry it as I carry everything, until it is clear what it is for, or until I am clear. Whichever comes first.

neutral: I accept. I do not understand. The two are not in conflict. I have accepted much of the Wall without understanding it.
disliked: This burns, or it rots, or it glitters. We have had enough of all three. Take it back, please.
I would rather you had brought nothing. Nothing, at least, dishonours nobody.
*sets it down far from the lanterns* Thank you for the thought. The thought I will keep. The thing, I will not.
You meant well, I am sure. The dead have heard that before. They are tired of it, and so am I.
Not this. Not in a Vigil. We have burned and we have rotted. We remember both too well already.

disliked.text: A gold ingot. The Piglins wore this to tell friend from foe, because nobody else would. I am nobody else. Please remove it before something remembers the War.
A nugget. Small, but it holds the whole of the Hoard in its shine. I have to look away. I do not mean to be rude. I mean to be safe.
That makes fire when asked. Our fires come lit and stay. Anything that begins a fire on request has the wrong idea about fire. Please put it away.
A fire charge. A ghast's fireball in a pocket. I will not ask why you carry it, because I would have to remember the answer. Put it where it cannot be seen.
A bucket of lava, in a place of lanterns. I thank you for the thought and not the bucket. The Magmari might want it. I am not a Magmari, and I do not ferry.
That is the shape of an ending. Take it far from the Wall. Farther. Then, when you think you are far enough, take it a little farther than that.
Rotten flesh. The Rotted wear it, I am told. We keep our dead better: by name, so they do not rot. Please take it away.
A ghast's tear. Some Ghastkin's, once. I do not wish to hold someone's grief like a coin. Put it down gently, and walk away from it with respect.
A bed. Here. You carry a thing that goes off like a ghast's fireball and offer it kindly. I will take it outside, and then quite a long way outside.

disliked: You meant well. I will say it again, so that it becomes true by repetition. You meant well. There. It is almost working.

disliked.text: No thank you! It is scary! The grown-ups would say it is not for me, and also not for them, and also not for the Hall.
That is the sort of thing grown-ups say never to touch. I touched it, in my head, and felt bad. So I am giving it back.
Ugh. I do not want it. Thank you for the thought. Take the rest away.
A brewer's bench is for clean things. This is not clean. I will accept the thought, but not the object.
I carve valley bone and nothing else. This is not valley bone, and it is not even bone. Take it back to wherever it came from.
My lanes burn soul fire, and I would rather add nothing that burns the other way. Keep it away from the posts, please.
Not near the terraces. Not near the wart. Wart is gentle and holds a grudge. I do not wish to be the cause.
I cannot accept this at the post. It is too near the sort of thing I am here to stop. You understand. I know you understand.
I will have to write this down as a refusal. A refusal is also a record. It will say you meant well and I did not accept. Both are true.
From you, I can forgive it. From anyone else I would have called the Ashwardens. You see how fond I am?

again: You have given already. Once is a gift. Twice starts to feel like a debt.
Keep it for another visit. I am still deciding where to put the last one.
Thank you, but no. Generosity is a thing to spread out, like candles.
Again? You will make me feel I owe you. I would rather owe you slowly.
Another? Slow down. Generosity is like wart: it grows best when you do not stand over it.
I have only one pair of hands, and they are full of you already. Come back when I have put the last one down.
One gift per visit. It is a custom I have just invented, and I am enforcing it at once. I am ashamed of how much I enjoy it.
You are very kind. Please be kind more slowly. I am still saying thank you for the last, and it takes me a while.
I cannot take another so soon. My shelf is full and my face is out of expressions.

again.text: You already gave me a present! If you give me two, I will have to share, and I am not ready.
I can only be happy about one thing at a time. I am still on the first. It is a very big happy.
I have no cup big enough for a second. Come back when the first has steeped.
A second gift means a second carving in return, and I have not finished the first. A carver does not rush gratitude.
Two gifts and one hand. I cannot hold a lantern, a gift and a gift. Come back when I have set one of them down.
You have given me enough for now. Let it settle. Gifts, like wart, are better spaced.
On duty I may accept one. Two is a bribe. I am not offended. I only have to pretend I am.
I have marked the first on my stole. A second would need another mark, and I have run out of room for happiness.
You are always welcome, and so are your gifts. But I am pacing myself, the way you pace a good brew. Come back soon without anything, and see how that feels.
A friend does not need to give twice. A friend's first gift lasts a long time. Yours is still on my shelf, and doing very well.
You have done enough for me. Sit down and be given something for a change. I have nothing small to hand, so I will sit with you. It is the better gift anyway.

again: Once is generosity. Twice is a habit. Three times is a debt. I would rather stay at generosity for now, if you do not mind.
Your hand is generous. My shelf is not. Save it for later; it will still be a gift then.

again.text: I have nowhere to put a second thing out here. I have my pocket and a rock. The pocket is full. The rock I am fond of.

again: Thank you, truly, but the first is still warm. I would like to give it a little more time before I begin another.
empty: Your hand is empty. That is fine. So is a lantern, before it is lit.
There is nothing in your hand. Did you mean to give me a moment of silence? I accept.
An empty hand. We greet the dead with those. I do hope that is not what you mean.
Nothing? Well. You came. That is a gift too, of a sort. A small one.
Your hand is empty. Do not apologise. The best visitors arrive with nothing in their hands and stay a long while.
Nothing in your hand? A good start. You have room for whatever comes.
You have come to give me nothing. That is a restful thing to be given.
Are you showing me that you carry no weapon, or that you carry no wart? Either is acceptable.
I looked at your hand, and your hand looked back. It was an honest meeting. We have agreed to say nothing.

empty.text: You forgot to bring something! That is all right. I forget my own things all the time. I forgot my name once. It came back.
Your hand's empty. Can I hold it? Not for anything. Just to see what it feels like.
If you had something in there, would it have been a secret? I like it better empty, when I can imagine.
An empty hand and an empty bottle, the two best friends of a brewer. Fill one, and the other will follow.
Nothing in your hand? I can work with that. A carver sees the shape in the nothing, and cuts around it.
An empty hand is a wick before the flame. It will catch. Everything catches, in time, if you are patient.
An empty hand is good for planting. You may leave something behind and not notice. I will notice.
I was told to watch the hands. Yours are empty and in plain sight. That is the best I have had at the post in a long while.
Empty hands are easy to read. Nothing to hide, nothing to carry. I could write you in one line.
You need bring nothing. I have said it before and I will say it again: you are enough of a visit by yourself.
I would rather you came with nothing and stayed a while. The silence we share is better than any gift in my pocket.
Empty, and you came anyway. That is the whole reason I keep you.

empty: I do not mind. A gift given on time is good; a gift given for the sake of giving is only a pause in a nicer coat.
Do not worry. A long talk is a gift of its own, and I have all the time in the world. It only takes more of it.

empty.text: Out here nobody has anything in their hands. We are all in the same condition. It is a fair place.

levelup.text: I said your name aloud just now, to the lanterns. Named Once. Most outsiders never get further.
Spoken Twice. The second time is the one that means it. Take this wart, from the terraces. Plant it on soul sand. Be patient.
Written in Ash. Your name is on my hearthstone now. Take these lanterns. Light them for whoever you have lost, and say their name each time.
Carved in Bone. That does not wear off. Take this soul fire for your own hearth. Sit by it. Say names. You will find you have more than you thought.
Kept. When you die, I will keep your name. And take this: it points to where you last fell. We use them to find our dead. Now you can find yours.
I said your name to the Wall. Only to hear how it sounds. It sounds alright.
You are my second favourite outsider now. I only know two. Here, I swept these up from the Bonecarver's floor.
I wrote your name in the ash with my finger. I am not supposed to write on things. I wrote it small. Here, have some of my torches.
I tried to carve your name into a bone. It came out as a skull. Most things do. Have it anyway.
At my first Vigil I might choose you, if you have died by then. Please do not hurry. Here, light this for me while you wait.
Named Once. I said your name to {kept} just now, so they would know who is calling. They did not object. Take these candles, and pinch them out when you are done.
Named Once. It sounds small, but nobody on the Wall began larger. Your name is in my mouth now. Do not worry. I keep it clean.
That is one hearing of your name, from me. The second has to be earned. It takes patience and a little ash. We have both.
I said your name three times, quietly, to see if it would fit in my mouth. It does! Here, I found this torch. It is not stolen. It is borrowed forever.
You are the one who comes back. I am going to tell the Wall: the one who comes back. It is a good name for you. I am very good at names.
Spoken Twice. I said your name to the Wall, and again to myself, so it would hold. Take this soul sand. Grow wart on it, and think of us whenever it sulks.
Two times now. The first was for hearing, the second for meaning. I do not say a name a third time lightly, so be careful what you do with the second.
Spoken Twice. The Remembrancer asked who you were, and I said, a friend of the lanes. I have never said that of anyone. I am still checking it is true.
I told the Cairnback about you! It did not say anything, but it moved a little closer, which for a Cairnback is like shouting.
I wrote your name on a bone bead and hid it under my bedroll with the secret one. Now I have two secrets, and you are one. Have these bottles. The Brewer has hundreds.
Written in Ash. Not on the Wall, only on my hearthstone, but that is nearer than most get. Take this tag. Name something with it. A name is the kindest gift for a creature that has none.
Written in Ash. I must be careful now: ash smudges, and so do friendships. I will take care. So, please, will you.
I told the Remembrancer I had put you in ash. They nodded. That nod is the nearest they come to a cheer. Enjoy it quietly.
Your name is in ash on the step by my home. There is no rain in the Nether, so it never washes out. Grown-ups say it is the only good thing about the weather.
I counted to Three for you, even the soft bit, and I did not hurry the Three. That makes you officially important.
Carved in Bone. Bone is slow to carve and slower to wear away. You are on my list of things that last. Take this wither rose. It grows where something has ended.
Carved in Bone. I do not say it to flatter. It is a fact of craft. I will not rub you out, and I will not soften you. I will keep you sharp.
Four times your name has come easily to me. The fifth is for the Wall. Do not rush me. I am coming to it.
I carved your name on a bone but ran out of bone. So it says the first half. The second half is still in the bone, waiting.
You are on my list now. Very near the top. Do not tell the others on the list. They might want to be near the top too.
Kept. I have put your name beside {kept}'s in my mouth. They seem to like the company. They are the best kind: they do not argue.
Kept. Here is a book to write your own names in. Copy mine if you like; the originals stay with me. Names are best kept in more than one place.
Kept. There is nothing more I can give that I have not given. I could offer my name, but then I would be nameless, and that is a calamity for a Withren. So: stay.
You are Kept! That is the highest one! I made you a lantern out of a jar and a candle. It leaks light a bit. Everything good leaks a bit.
When I choose, I might choose someone you know. Then you can visit them. That would be so many names in one place!

farewell.text: Bye! Do not die! Or if you do, tell me first, so I can choose you.
Bye. I will tell the Wall you visited. It does not answer, but I think it likes to know.
Go. I will watch the lane until you are off it. It is my job, and also I want to.
Go well. I have your face now. I do not lose faces.
Go on. The valley is wide, and most of it is someone.
Go well, friend. I will tell {kept} you left in good health. They will be relieved. They worry, for someone who cannot.

farewell: Go carefully. Come back with the same name you left with.
Walk well. Mind the soul sand. It holds on to things.
Farewell. I will say your name once after you have gone, to see if it stays.
Go, then. The lanterns will still be lit. They are always lit. That is rather the point.
Until next time. There is always a next time, until there is not. Then there is the Wall.
Keep your skulls apart and your fires small. That is all the advice we have, and it is plenty.
Leave when you like. The lantern will still be here, and so, probably, will I.
Mind the ash on your way out. It likes to follow people.
Go. I will keep your place as it was. It is the only way anyone finds it again.
